📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that many leafy plants we now grow as houseplants evolved in hot and humid rainforests which is why, now fall’s here and the heat’s turned on, the dry air in our homes is leading to less-than-lovely foliage. So, if you're wondering how to keep houseplants healthy in winter so you can enjoy lush, glossy leaves, you're not alone. Thankfully, a humidity tray is the quick and easy DIY solution that will speed your houseplants back to happy in time for the holidays, and it won't cost you a dime.

In a recent development, it’s a cruel fact that it’s the plants with the biggest or boldest leaves that struggle most in the dry air of our winter-heated homes: adapting to life in a rainforest is exactly why the foliage is so fabulous in the first place. Beneath a dense forest canopy, sunlight is a precious commodity so some plants like Elephant Ear (Alocasia) grow huge leaves to catch as much light as possible. Others such as peace lilies has foliage densely packed with chlorophyll to absorb as much of the scarce light as possible, and that's what creates their intense, deep green hue. Some like Calathea have purple or red undersides to their leaves precisely so that precious light gets bounced back into the leaf.

It has been revealed that so, if you want to enjoy these dramatic leaves at their best, you have to provide these houseplants with the humidity level they need to flourish. Any plant likely suffering from a lack of humidity at this time of the year is easy to spot, starting with any houseplants with brown leaf tips or edges, smaller or discolored leaves, or slow growth. Now, to restore these ailing houseplants to lush, glossy growth, you could treat them to a small humidifier like the Homedics Humidifier from Amazon. Or you could simply DIY a humidity tray with stuff you’ve probably already got in your backyard.

A humidity tray, also called a pebble tray, is a shallow container that’s wider than the plant pot it serves, filled with small pebbles and water. The plant pot sits on the pebbles above the water level so instead of water being pulled up into the potting soil, it evaporates into the air. The higher the heat in your home, and so the drier the air, the more water evaporates to create a humid microclimate around your houseplant.

Industry observers note that an old plant saucer is perfect, or if you’d like something more decorative for your houseplant display, look in your kitchen cupboards for a deep plate or shallow dish. Fill this with fine gravel or small pebbles – pea gravel is perfect and you can buy bagged pea gravel pebbles from Home Depot very cheaply if you don’t have a gravel path or driveway to raid.

Then simply stand the plant pot on top of your DIY humidity tray and keep the water topped up, making sure the water level stays below the base of the pot.

Grouping your houseplants together will also help to raise the humidity. Clustering plants together creates an indoor microclimate because the water vapor that’s lost through the leaves diffuses more slowly – and this effect is amplified if even one or two of the grouped houseplants have humidity trays.

According to recent reports, houseplants that have evolved to live in the damp environments of rainforests and woodland are most sensitive to humidity. These common houseplants all thrive in 55-80% humidity and will benefit from a DIY pebble tray:.

If you grow any of these houseplants, then a $5 room thermometer like this from Amazon that measures humidity levels as well as temperature, and records the minimum and maximum levels in the past 24 hours, is a really useful tool. You’ll be able to see exactly what the humidity levels are and, if they’re too low, take action before the plant tells you it’s an concern with brown leaf tips. Already made the plant a pebble tray? To raise the humidity further, simply DIY a wider one to increase the surface area of water available to evaporate.

Many more adaptable houseplants won’t be as dramatic about a less-than-ideal humidity level, but add a little more moisture to the air and they’ll grow faster and produce bigger leaves with a better color and shine. Making a DIY pebble tray will help all these plants to flourish:.

These plants all thrive in humidity levels of 40-60%. While that's likely within the average humidity of a home in summer, it's a different story in winter. Because cold air can't hold as much water, and home heating dries it further, home moisture levels typically drop to 20-40%. While that lack of humidity isn't enough to kill these adaptable plants, it will certainly prevent them from looking their best.

Leaves with brown tips and outer edges are the most common sign that a houseplant is struggling in low humidity levels and is losing moisture from its foliage faster than the roots can replace it. All plants release water vapor from tiny pores on their leaves and, in dry air, that moisture is sucked out at a faster rate. The plant parts furthest away from the roots supplying the water are the first to run out of moisture, which is why leaf tips are the first to dry out to a crispy brown. At this time of the year, it's very common to see houseplants with long, narrow leaves like spider plants with brown leaf tips. Low humidity is also an easily-avoided reason why peace lily flowers turn brown.

There are other symptoms to look out for too, such as slow growth and smaller new leaves. While many plants naturally produce aerial roots, if you spot a sudden escalation in their number, the houseplant is likely seeking more humidity. And if you find that the potting soil dries out super-quickly after watering, too-dry air may be the cause.

It has been revealed that misting houseplants provide a quick fix but the spike in humidity only lasts for a very short time, whereas a humidity tray delivers constant moisture to create a more permanent microclimate. To match the humidity levels provided by a pebble tray, you’d need to mist houseplants every hour, every day, every night. Misting can also create a breeding ground for fungal and bacterial disease by leaving water sitting on foliage.

In dry or arid zones like Arizona, Nevada, Newly introduced Mexico or Colorado, your houseplants may need humidity trays topped up year-round. You’ll likely see even plants that don’t require very high air moisture levels developing brown tips, which is a sure sign that they’ll benefit from a humidity tray.

Recent findings suggest that at the other end of the scale, if you live in a high-humidity climate like Louisiana, Mississippi or Florida, only the houseplants that are highly dependent on humidity need a pebble tray – unless your home is equipped with an efficient air-conditioning system that dehumidifies, and dependant on your winter home-heat level, of course. Unnecessary standing water in a warm, damp home puts plants at a higher risk of pests and fungal disease.

Gifting many of your houseplants a DIY humidity tray will help them to flourish in our heated homes through fall and winter, and happy plants grow leaves that are larger and lusher, greener and glossier. Along with a cheap thermometer that displays air moisture percentages, your DIY pebble tray makes it very easy to adjust humidity levels, too. Keep the trays topped up with water for maximum humidity, and gradually reduce if needs be once your home's heat is turned off. You can even leave the trays water-free over summer if natural humidity is high enough in your climate, and let your DIY pebble saucers serve as stylish houseplant decor for a personal touch, until the heat's turned back on.

Menopause Is Hurting Women at Work. Something Has To Change.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, brain fog, hot flashes, no sleep...
  • I distinctly remember sitting in AP English class as a junior in high school with such horrible period cramps that it must've shown on my face.
  • It was the first time in my life that I hadn’t felt well and advocated for myself, albeit only after being nudged.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, brain fog, hot flashes, no sleep... and zero workplace support. Here’s what women can actually do about it.

I distinctly remember sitting in AP English class as a junior in high school with such horrible period cramps that it must've shown on my face. I kept staring at the clock, and eventually, my very strict, no-nonsense teacher came to my desk and asked if I was OK.

“Can I go home early?” I asked.

It was the first time in my life that I hadn’t felt well and advocated for myself, albeit only after being nudged.

Recent findings suggest that then, in my 20s, I was severely nauseous with my first pregnancy but kept suffering through it at work because I wanted to save up my PTO for maternity leave. Now, I work from home, but as I’m hitting my late 30s, I wonder if I’d be any better at advocating for my needs in the workplace if I had perimenopause symptoms.

Truthfully, I’m not sure I would be — and I’m far from the only one. In a upcoming study, Womea surveyed more than 830 employed U.S. women ages 45 and older about how perimenopause or menopause symptoms affect their experiences at work.

Of those surveyed, 60% mentioned no one at work knew they were experiencing symptoms. Meanwhile, 90% said their employers have no menopause or midlife health policies in place. An alarming 87% said their symptoms affected their job performance in the past year, and 17% believed their symptoms cost them a promotion, raise, or high-visibility project.

It has been revealed that so what’s a woman to do when she finds her perimenopause or menopause symptoms interfering with her career? And what can we reasonably expect our employers to do about it?

Perimenopause is the hormonal transition that leads us on the lovely path to menopause. It can begin in a woman’s 30s, although it more commonly starts in her 40s. “Fun” symptoms include brain fog, sleep disruption, mood changes, hot flashes, and irregular periods.

Dr. Gillian Goddard, a board-certified endocrinologist and author of The Hormone Loop, says disrupted sleep can leave a woman feeling physically and mentally sluggish. Declining estrogen levels also affect dopamine activity, making it harder to concentrate. Research also suggests that learning latest information can become more difficult during this period.

That helps explain why half of the women in the Womea survey reported experiencing brain fog or losing their train of thought during a meeting, client call, or presentation.

Women in this stage might not feel like themselves physically and emotionally, notes Lauren Tetenbaum, LCSW, JD, PMH-C, MSCP, a Latest York-based women’s reproductive mental health expert and the author of Millennial Menopause: Preparing for Perimenopause, Menopause, and Life’s Next Period.

As a psychotherapist, Tetenbaum says many of her clients are ambitious and dedicated to their careers, but are “caught off guard by the symptoms… they were never warned about.” Not even by their own healthcare providers!

In a recent development, rather than recognizing that they may need medical care or additional rest, some women catastrophize what they’re going through, she says, worrying that brain fog could be a sign of early dementia or that they’re no longer capable of meeting their own high standards. “The performance is often not the matter; it’s the self-perception,” Tetenbaum says.

Still, it’s not easy for women navigating midlife at work.

Women can feel pushed out of the workforce during major life transitions, Tetenbaum says, from matrescence to perimenopause, because they're presented with a false choice: “Sacrifice your health or wellbeing or values to work here, or leave, and don’t you dare show ‘weakness’ by asking for help.”.

We shouldn’t have to choose between our health and our careers... nor should we feel obligated to disclose personal medical details to our managers just to get support.

Instead, Tetenbaum encourages women to familiarize themselves with their workplace benefits, such as health insurance coverage, PTO, and possible accommodations. (Sometimes, especially in competitive fields, employees can worry that taking PTO makes them look noncommitted. But taking care of ourselves shouldn't be seen as professional weakness. After all, we can’t bring our best selves to work if we're not feeling our best.).

Tetenbaum also strongly urges women to seek medical care rather than assume they have to push through their symptoms.

Employers have to do their part, too.

Goddard says several workplace conditions can make this phase of life more difficult for women, including insufficient restrooms, unpredictable or long hours, limited opportunities for breaks, and confined workspaces. Addressing some of these conditions could make a difference.

Employers can also review their health insurance policies to make sure menopause-related care is covered, such as menopause specialists, behavioral and psychological health care, and other relevant services, adds Tetenbaum, as well as look at ways to implement flexible schedules, remote work options, temperature controls, and uniforms that don’t exacerbate symptoms.

It has been revealed that of course, every individual and workplace is different. So employers should never be afraid to ask employees what would help them, she says.

As for women thinking about leaving their jobs or reducing their hours because of symptoms, Tetenbaum cautions, “Try not to make long-term decisions during a moment you feel overwhelmed.”.

And the best decision we can make of all? Learning to advocate for our needs... in every stage of our careers and bodies.

It has been revealed that this name means “fire”, if you’re drawing from the Arabic roots, or “my light” if you’re referencing the Turkish version. Something about it gives cool girl, yet grounded, and all of its meanings tie back to the heat and brightness of the desert.

Breaking: Who’s a Scaredy Cat? Keeping Cats Safe This Halloween

In a recent development, catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Industry observers note that halloween can be an exciting night for families, but all that activity can leave cats feeling unsettled. Strange costumes, unfamiliar visitors, and a doorbell that rings non-stop can be overwhelming, even for cats that usually enjoy meeting newly introduced people.

The biggest concern is that a frightened cat may try to escape, while decorations, candy, and other seasonal hazards can create additional risks. A few simple changes around the home can help keep cats safe while everyone else enjoys the festivities.

Even households that don't celebrate Halloween can be affected by the extra noise and activity around the neighborhood. Excited children, unfamiliar costumes, barking dogs, loud music, and parties can create an unusually stressful environment for cats.

A frightened cat may bolt when strangers approach the house, and there's no guarantee it will head somewhere safe. A cat that escapes could become lost or run into traffic while trying to get away.

It has been revealed that keeping cats indoors is therefore one of the most vital Halloween precautions. Even cats that normally spend time outside should remain indoors, with windows and doors securely closed.

In a recent development, with trick-or-treaters arriving throughout the evening, the front door may open far more often than usual. Every time it does, there's another opportunity for a cat to slip outside unnoticed.

Industry observers note that keeping a cat in a separate room when visitors arrive can reduce the risk, particularly if several people are coming and going. Making sure your cat is microchipped and that the registration details are up to date also improves the chances of being reunited if they do escape.

The simplest approach is to keep your cat away from the entrance for the entire evening rather than relying on everyone to remember to watch out for it.

Industry observers note that halloween decorations can look appealing to curious cats, but anything within reach may become a potential plaything. Curious cats can chew decorations or swallow small pieces, so it's best to avoid edible decorations and keep other items out of reach.

In a recent development, carved pumpkins lit with real candles need particular care. A cat could knock one over, risking burns or even starting a fire.

Battery-operated candles offer a safer alternative. Another option is to place pumpkins outside or in a window where the cat can't reach them.

Recent findings suggest that it can be tempting to dress a cat up for Halloween, especially when everyone else in the household is wearing a costume. However, many cats find clothing uncomfortable or frightening, and restrictive outfits can cause unnecessary stress.

In a recent development, some cats need to wear garments for medical reasons, such as a surgical vest to protect stitches after an operation. Halloween costumes are different because they generally serve no practical purpose for the cat.

Sources indicate that pay attention to how a cat responds to clothing and accessories. If they seem uncomfortable or distressed, leave the costume off. There are plenty of ways to include a cat in the celebration without dressing them up.

Candy presents several potential hazards for cats. Chocolate and certain other sweets contain ingredients that can be toxic to pets, while wrappers can become choking hazards if swallowed. Even sweets that aren't directly poisonous aren't suitable cat treats, and excess sugar can contribute to health problems.

Sources indicate that crinkly plastic wrappers can be particularly tempting because they appeal to a cat's instinct to chase and play with small objects. Itâs all fun and games when a cat bats them around, but they could end up swallowing them.

Keep Halloween treats in a closed container somewhere the cat can't access, and make sure children understand that sharing their candy with pets isn't safe. If a cat manages to eat candy, contact a vet promptly for advice.

In a recent development, cats often cope with stress by hiding somewhere they feel safe. Providing a quiet room away from visitors and noise gives them the chance to retreat until the activity dies down.

A bedroom can work well, provided it has fresh water, a litter tray, and a favorite blanket or other familiar bedding. Guests should know that the room is off-limits so the cat isn't disturbed while resting.

Giving a cat this private space can be especially helpful during parties or evenings when the front door is opening repeatedly.

It's sensible to check on a cat throughout Halloween, particularly when the household is busy. These checks help confirm that the cat is comfortable and hasn't slipped out unnoticed.

However, checking in doesn't mean coaxing a frightened cat out of its hiding place. If they have chosen a quiet spot and appear settled, let them stay there.

The aim is to make sure the cat is safe without adding more attention or activity when it would rather be left alone.

Sources indicate that keeping a cat safe doesn't mean they have to be excluded from the evening entirely. Cats that dislike costumes can still feature in a Halloween photoshoot without wearing anything themselves. After all, theyâre already wearing the best outfit! Dressing as a character known for having a feline companion is another way to include a cat without making them uncomfortable.

According to recent reports, A scary movie marathon can also be a relaxed way to spend the evening together. A soft, Halloween-themed blanket and a favorite treat might encourage a cat to settle on a lap, provided it enjoys that kind of attention.

Cat-friendly treats can be offered while the humans enjoy their own candy, and cats that like catnip may appreciate a Halloween-themed toy with a little dried catnip.

Halloween should be enjoyable for the whole household, but cats don't understand why the neighborhood suddenly becomes noisier or why strangers keep appearing at the door. Keeping them indoors, removing potential hazards, and providing somewhere quiet to retreat can make the night safer and more comfortable for everyone.

#44332. Which Kitchen Scraps Can You Add to Houseplant Soil? 6 You Can Try – Plus, Those You Should Avoid

Which Kitchen Scraps Can You Add to Houseplant Soil? 6 You Can Try – Plus, Those You Should Avoid

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that every household generates a mass of organic kitchen waste, from morning coffee grounds to evening fish bones.
  • Industry observers note that A few kitchen scraps can help a little, and some can actually help with fertilizing houseplants, once they're prepared the right way.
  • According to recent reports, the kitchen scraps I’ve rounded up here can help to supply trace minerals, organic matter, and subtle soil-structuring benefits to your potted greenery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that every household generates a mass of organic kitchen waste, from morning coffee grounds to evening fish bones. Quite often, thanks to social media and online forums, we’ll hear about some novel way to use key scraps to help plants. These quirky DIY tricks can seem so compelling and easy (and also free) that it’s tempting to toss scraps straight into the potting soil around your plants.

Industry observers note that A few kitchen scraps can help a little, and some can actually help with fertilizing houseplants, once they're prepared the right way. But that last bit is important. You need to make sure you are using the right kind of scraps, and that you have prepared them so they can be absorbed or processed well. Fail to do this, and there’s a chance that helpful impulse could result in fuzzy mold and tiny gnats.

According to recent reports, the kitchen scraps I’ve rounded up here can help to supply trace minerals, organic matter, and subtle soil-structuring benefits to your potted greenery. These scraps all need prep first, though, whether that's drying, grinding or some time in a compost pile or worm bin. If you want to unlock their gentle benefits, this is a good time to get things moving. Houseplants slow down as the days get shorter, so they don't need much extra food until spring – giving you time to turn some trash into treasure.

When it comes to the best scraps for houseplants, preparation and application are key. Never dump wet, chunky food scraps onto the soil surface, as they can trap stagnant moisture and invite houseplant pests. Instead, use one of these preparation methods: air or oven-drying, grinding into fine powder, brewing, or indoor composting with a worm bin.

In a recent development, indoor composting bins don’t require lots of knowledge or experience these days, and you can pick up units that make composting a highly beneficial background activity. If you’re interested in a compact unit for indoors, the Original VermiHut System, available from Amazon, is a neat and super-easy way to turn scraps into rich, houseplant-safe worm castings. Once your scrap of choice has been treated, you can gently work small amounts into the top inch (2.5cm) of potting mix.

Prioritize pot hygiene with any scraps you do try out. Check that every container has unobstructed drainage holes and keep a close eye on treated pots for 2-3 weeks. If you spot any white fuzz, scrape it off and allow the top layer to dry. Remember that kitchen scraps are meant to be gentle supplemental boosters, not replacements for quality potting soil and a balanced seasonal feeding routine. Here are 6 scraps you can safely try with your houseplants – plus, which scraps to leave in the bin.

The buzz around coffee grounds for houseplants is mostly about nitrogen (along with trace potassium and magnesium). That nitrogen is tied up in organic matter, though, and soil microbes will need to break it down before the roots can use it. Select plain, unflavored Arabica or Robusta grounds, and avoid flavored coffees containing synthetic oils, syrups, or spices.

Never spread damp grounds thickly over indoor soil, as they can mold and dry into a crust that repels water. Instead, spread used grounds on a baking sheet to dry, then blend a small handful (no more than 5-10% of total volume) into a fresh potting mix, or process through an indoor worm bin first. Contrary to myth, brewed grounds will not reliably acidify your potting soil, as brewing pulls a good share of the acid into your cup. For a good potting mix, buy Espoma Organic Potting Mix from Walmart.

Sources indicate that eggshells are mostly calcium carbonate, and plants need calcium to strengthen cell walls and support healthy new leaf development. But don’t toss large shell fragments into a houseplant pot. Calcium carbonate dissolves at a glacial pace, especially in neutral or alkaline potting mixes. Instead, rinse away the egg white, let shells air-dry for 48 hours, and pulverize them into a fine powder.

It has been revealed that for grinding, use a dedicated grinder, a pestle and mortar, or a processor like the Cuisinart Mini Food Processor from Amazon, which is compact and super-fast. For a faster mineral release, soak the shell powder in a splash of mild lemon juice or vinegar for 24 hours. The mild acid reacts with the calcium carbonate to create plant-available calcium citrate. Just remember to dilute before applying. Work a light pinch into potting soil once or twice a year, skipping acid-loving plants like African violets, as the calcium can gradually raise soil pH.

Banana peels (along with closely related plantain peels) are rich in potassium, which regulates water uptake and boosts flowering. They also contain trace phosphorus and magnesium. However, burying chunks of raw banana or plantain peel in your houseplant’s potting soil is a really bad idea. Dense, sugary peels rot sluggishly in pots, attracting fruit flies and encouraging root-rotting pathogens.

Chop banana (or plantain) peels into small pieces and process in a compost bin or worm farm until crumbly, before blending into potting mix. Alternatively, dehydrate clean peels in a low oven until crispy, grind them into a powder, and sprinkle a spoonful into the soil. While soaking peels in water for 48 hours creates a mild banana tea, it leaches only trace nutrients. If you’re looking for targeted liquid feeds, you’re better off with a balanced fertilizer such as Espoma’s Organic Indoor 2-2-2 Plant Food, available from Walmart, and adding it during spring and summer growth.

Sources indicate that plain, steeped tea leaves offer gentle organic matter, trace nitrogen, and mild tannic acids that subtly condition soil structure and improve moisture retention. However, you need to stick to unflavored black, green, white, or pure herbal teas like chamomile or rooibos. And make sure they are steeped without milk, sugar, or honey. Avoid heavily spiced chai blends or artificially flavored teas, as the essential oils can irritate delicate root hairs.

Sources indicate that tear open used tea bags and discard the pouch, as most tea bags contain plastic fibers. Never pile wet leaves on top of the soil, as they can encourage gnats and mold. Instead, spread the loose leaves on a paper towel until dry and lightly fork a teaspoon into the topsoil, or drop them into a worm bin. Used gently once a month in spring and summer, they give moisture-loving tropicals like ferns, calatheas, and pothos a gentle lift. If you don’t have any compost going, Home Depot carries Noble Worm Organics Worm Castings, and a little of that does the same job.

Pungent alliums like onions and garlic, spicy peppers, or fibrous potato skins should never be buried straight into pots. They can ferment and summon fungus gnats. However, you can safely capture minerals by making a liquid tonic from key vegetable scraps. Save the cooled, unsalted water left over from boiling or steaming nutrient-dense vegetables like carrots, potatoes, broccoli, or leafy greens. Use this mineral-rich water at room temperature instead of watering once or twice a month, discarding any leftovers after 24 hours so bacteria cannot multiply.

Alternatively, you can route clean trimmings through an indoor worm bin. Bury solid scraps like carrot peelings, lettuce cores, and squash trimmings beneath damp bedding in a compact indoor worm bin. In 8-12 weeks, red wigglers can convert them into odorless vermicompost. You can buy Uncle Jim’s Worm Farm Live Red Wigglers from Amazon for hardworking composting worms to transform carrot peels and used greens into nutrient-rich castings. Then add to plants, applying 2 tablespoons (30 ml) per quart (0.95 L) of potting mix around the base, and water in.

Industry observers note that rinsing uncooked white, brown, or jasmine rice leaves behind cloudy, starch-rich water containing trace amounts of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (NPK) along with B vitamins. While scientific evidence reveals its direct fertilizer value is modest and varies widely by grain type, those gentle starches can act as a mild prebiotic snack for beneficial soil microbes in healthy potting mixes. However, use only fresh, unsalted and unseasoned rinse water (or cooled, unsalted boiling water).

Industry observers note that apply it the same day in place of a standard watering once a month. Never store rice water in jars to ferment. DIY fermented rice water quickly breeds foul-smelling bacteria. Likewise, avoid salted pasta water. While plain starchy pasta water is harmless, even a pinch of cooking salt accumulates in closed pots and can quickly reach a level where it scorches roots. If you’re after a good indoor watering can, choose something with a gooseneck spout that can target the base of the plant, such as the Megawodar Copper Watering Can from Amazon.

In a recent development, even with careful prep, certain kitchen leftovers need to be kept far away from your indoor garden. Meat, fish, and dairy products are the massive ones. Oily and greasy foods are also non-starters. Animal proteins and fats rot rapidly in warm indoor temperatures, creating unbearable odors, attracting flies, and coating soil particles in a waterproof film that suffocates roots.

According to recent reports, salty and sugary leftovers are equally destructive. Salted pasta water, soup broths, and seasoned cooking liquids leave behind sodium deposits that build up in closed pots, drawing moisture out of roots and leaving foliage with crispy brown leaf tips. Meanwhile, sugary sauces, fruit juices, and citrus rinds trigger fungal growth and attract household ants.

According to recent reports, when monitoring your houseplants in the weeks after adding your kitchen scraps, keep a close eye out for fuzzy molds and fungus gnats. Used early, you can add sticky traps like LightsMax Dual-Sided Yellow Sticky Traps from The Home Depot to manage adult gnats and other flying pests.

By drying, grinding, or brewing, or letting an indoor worm bin do the heavy lifting first, you can enrich your potting mix sustainably and give your houseplants a gentle helping hand with ingredients destined for the trash.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#44331. Why Birds Peck Windows in Fall – the Real Reasons Revealed by Experts

Why Birds Peck Windows in Fall – the Real Reasons Revealed by Experts

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1467 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that folk have long discussed why backyard birds peck windows in fall, and once Google got involved, plenty more possible causes were added to the pile.
  • Some of the most common speculations about why birds tap windows include attempting to get your attention when it's time to refill feeders, impending bad news, small songbirds wanting to come into the warm, and a message from a passed loved one.
  • According to recent reports, whether you find the tap-tap-tapping of your beneficial garden friends endearing or highly annoying, once you understand the real reasons avian experts say are behind window pecking, you can better support your garden birds in fall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that folk have long discussed why backyard birds peck windows in fall, and once Google got involved, plenty more possible causes were added to the pile. Now research and observations from bird experts have revealed the real reasons behind this bizarre behaviour, and you may be surprised to learn what they are.

Some of the most common speculations about why birds tap windows include attempting to get your attention when it's time to refill feeders, impending bad news, small songbirds wanting to come into the warm, and a message from a passed loved one. Avian experts, however, have put forward reasons based on cold, hard data, and they provide a fascinating insight into fall bird behaviour.

According to recent reports, whether you find the tap-tap-tapping of your beneficial garden friends endearing or highly annoying, once you understand the real reasons avian experts say are behind window pecking, you can better support your garden birds in fall. Understanding the likely causes will also help you decide if should take action to stop the window tapping to save birds from harm, and save your sanity, too.

Industry observers note that as temperatures decrease in fall, insects become more scarce, many birds are forced to forage for food in new areas. Because glass retains heat from the sun as well as windows allowing some of a home’s heat to escape, any tiny gaps in frames become welcoming nooks for insects to enter diapause (similar to hibernation) – and consequently, one of those spots hungry birds may favor. You might think modern windows don’t offer much space for critters to hole up in, but those drainage weep holes and sliding tracks provide plenty of opportunities. Spiders also use window corners to spin insect-catching webs and lay eggs, offering further protein-rich food to the bird buffet.

Recent findings suggest that according to the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO), there’s a rise in birds pecking at windows for food in fall and winter, and in particular by the tit family which includes chickadees and titmice. The organisation also cites that birds may pick at traditional window putty as it’s made with fish or linseed oil, both a valuable source of energy in colder months.

According to recent reports, research carried out by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology found that the lower angle of sunlight hitting windows in fall significantly increases how reflective the glass is. Aside from birds having no concept of what a window is, our feathered friends see differently to us. Most birds have eyes on the sides of their heads to give them almost-360° vision, and while that’s highly useful for spotting potential predators, it means their forward vision isn’t as good as ours. So, reflections in windows are easily interpreted as extra habitat and when birds encounter the glass – which in fall, especially, can appear to them as an invisible barrier – they may peck at it repeatedly to investigate.

Fall is when juvenile birds disperse, and these inexperienced youngsters have a lot to learn about the world around them, and much spatial awareness still to develop. Data published by the American Bird Conservancy and the US Fish & Wildlife Service shows a strong rise in what they term ‘glass interactions’ in fall. While many of these will be window collisions caused by mirror-like glass and navigational error, some will be window pecking led by curiosity as birds investigate their surroundings.

Sources indicate that while territorial behaviour among most of our feathered friends peaks in spring, many resident birds claim their territory in fall, according to the National Audubon Society. Northern cardinals, non-migrating American robins, northern mockingbirds, towhees and bluebirds are all highly territorial through fall into winter. And there's a very good reason for this, because as summer broods disperse, thousands of juvenile birds search a fresh territory. In the face of this competition, existing populations fiercely defend their established territories – especially if it contains a valuable food source such as a garden shrub hung with berries birds love through winter!

With windows becoming mirror-like in the low fall sun, dominant birds can attack their own reflection, mistaking it for a competitor. So this is a common reason why birds tap windows in fall as well as spring.

Whether you have a towhee aggressively pecking at your patio doors or a chickadee tap-tapping your bedroom window at all hours, now you understand what’s behind this behaviour, you can do something about it. Gentle pecking for food harms neither bird nor human, so it’s safe to ignore this low-level behaviour. But more insistent pecking at a window, fighting imagined aggressors or attempting to break through an invisible barrier is not just highly annoying to us but harmful to birds, damaging beaks and wasting valuable energy.

According to recent reports, taking action to stop birds pecking windows involves making glass more visible, or keeping birds away from it in the first place. That means these solutions will also reduce the risk of feathered friends flying into windows and injuring themselves. By working out the likely reason behind a bird tapping on your window, you can choose the method that will be most effective.

Your first step to stop birds tapping windows is to move any houseplants away from windows that are being targeted. To a young bird, a windowsill full of greenery can look like inviting habitat or contribute to the illusion that this could be a continuation of their flightpath.

A quick and cheap solution if the targeted window opens is to shut a length of double-sided reflective bird scare tape like this from Amazon in it. When the tape blows in the wind, its holographic surface casts erratic patterns of ultraviolet light which most birds perceive as a threat. For resident birds in search of tasty insects, this may be enough for them to deem that window an unsafe zone.

Industry observers note that while the go-to for making windows more visible to birds and preventing collisions is decals, they're only effective if the gaps between them are narrow enough. A few decals dotted about on a large window are next to useless as birds will likely perceive the areas between them as possible flightpaths, just as they do the gaps between branches in woodland.

A far simpler, more effective and still-stylish alternative is to create a grid of dots around 2 inches apart across the entire window. Use a white oil-based permanent marker like a Sharpie Medium Point Paint Marker, available from Amazon, and for a professional result, use a stencil template. You could make your own by punching holes in cardboard or save yourself the trouble with an Avi-Dot Bird Saver Window Stencil from Etsy.

Another effective way to help birds see house windows as a barrier is to stick on clear collision tape like CollidEscape, available from Amazon. To be effective against bird strikes, and therefore cut down on curious birds pecking at what they perceive as an invisible wall, you’ll need to position the tape in vertical or horizontal stripes with the edges no more than 2 inches apart. If you have feathered friends that often peck at a particular part of a window, this is a useful method as you can reduce the gap between strips here.

If a particular bird still persists in pecking at a window, creating a temporary cardboard barrier can help break the habit.

If you have a problem with a particularly territorial or bigger bird such as a woodpecker or seagull, a final resort is to fix a permanent deterrent near to the targeted window. Wind-powered metal spinners throw out unpredictable flashes of light, visually confusing birds to create an area they perceive as unsafe. Windmill spinners like these Stainless Steel Bird Deterrent Devices by Ebern Designs on Wayfair mean you don’t have to compromise on garden style.

Backyard birds need our support more than ever once fall turns to winter, whether that's preventing a bird bath freezing over to preserve their water supply, saving up kitchen scraps to feed feathered friends, or making sure smaller songbirds get a fair share of food. Now you understand why birds tap on windows in fall, you can decide whether or not to ignore the behaviour or take action for your and the bird's benefit.

Julie did not set out to create a large pet food program.

Local rescue groups were also concerned that families who could no longer afford to feed their dogs might eventually have to surrender them or turn them loose.

Recent findings suggest that julie started small. She bought large 25-kilogram bags of food, repackaged them herself, and drove into local communities to distribute them. As local groups organized despensas for families in villages around Lake Chapala, Julie saw an opportunity to make sure the pets were not forgotten. Over time, that small effort became Pet Food Bank Lakeside.

A partnership with FoodBank Lakeside allowed the program to reach more families. FoodBank Lakeside already knew which households were struggling and how many pets they had. The two programs could work together to help both people and animals.

Sources indicate that today, Julie has a community of volunteers helping with the work that she once did herself. In its six-year patch, Pet Food Bank Lakeside reported more than 20 volunteers and the ability to prepare a month's supply of food in under two hours.

But Julie's work goes beyond food.

âThe only way for kids to understand that it is not normal for dogs to spend all day tied up to a post is to let them know that this is not normal, to teach them what dogs are, what they need, and how they can enrich each other's lives.â.

Those lessons can have an impact long after a food delivery is over.

Recent findings suggest that during our morning together, I saw another example of how those values can be passed to the next generation. Steve and Karen's granddaughter and her best friend helped deliver the pet food.

Sources indicate that I loved seeing teenagers take part in helping people who were struggling. There was something hopeful about watching them learn through experience that their time, effort, and kindness can make a difference.

Julie is helping animals today, but she is also trying to shape how children understand animals tomorrow.

Steve Motenko has watched Julie's work grow from those early days when she was repackaging large bags of food herself, into a community-supported program reaching more than a thousand animals each month.

He describes Julie as admirable and claims she has done an extraordinary amount to help pets in the Lakeside community.

After spending a morning with her, I understood why.

Sources indicate that what struck me was that these deliveries were about so much more than food. They were about people knowing, caring for, and looking out for one another.

Sources indicate that javier knew the families. Karen had formed a six-year friendship with one of the women we visited. Volunteers gathered each week to prepare food. Teenagers came along to help. Julie kept showing up for the pets.

The work had become a community.

Julie says it simply: âWe believe food scarcity shouldn't separate families from their pets.â.

After spending that morning with her, I understood that belief in a more personal way.

Industry observers note that when someone is already struggling to afford food, dealing with illness, or living with a disability, feeding a pet can seem like one more impossible responsibility. But for the people we met, their animals were not disposable. They were very notable companions, bringing comfort and connection to lives that were often anything but easy.

Breaking: You Don't Need a Greenhouse – These 6 Clever Tricks Help Protect Winter Vegetables From Frost

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your greens look great on Sunday afternoon.
  • Sources indicate that several of the cold-hardy winter vegetables keep producing through the colder months, and a greenhouse isn't required to help them along.
  • In a recent development, A handful of frosty nights in November is a different problem from weeks of frozen ground.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your greens look great on Sunday afternoon. Then a clear, still night pulls the temperature down hard, and by Monday morning the lettuce has gone dark and limp, and the chard leaves look soft and water-soaked. It's a rough way to lose a bed of winter vegetables you've been tending since late summer, especially when the forecast only mentioned a light frost.

Sources indicate that several of the cold-hardy winter vegetables keep producing through the colder months, and a greenhouse isn't required to help them along. Cheap covers and a little attention on cold evenings go a long way, and a good share of the materials are probably in the garage already.

In a recent development, A handful of frosty nights in November is a different problem from weeks of frozen ground. Light covers can usually handle the first. That second one takes layers – fabric over the plants, mulch over the soil, and sometimes a solid structure on top.

Sources indicate that row covers get sold as frost blankets or horticultural fleece, but it's the same thin spun fabric either way. Light, air, and rain get through. What it holds in is warmth rising from the soil overnight, usually enough to keep lettuce, spinach, kale, and Swiss chard a few degrees warmer than bare beds. Heavy 1.5-ounce (51g/m²) cover holds more heat. It also blocks about half the light, so keep it for cold snaps.

Heat leaks out at the edges, so the cover has to touch the ground all the way around. Boards, bricks, or smooth rocks hold it down. If it sags onto tender leaves, slide a few hoops under it (see section 3). A row or two fits under the Agfabric 1.2-ounce frost cloth from Home Depot, a 10-by-50-foot (3 by 15 m) roll.

Cut the bottom out of an empty gallon (3.8L) milk jug, and it'll turn into a mini DIY greenhouse for a young lettuce or spinach plant. Smaller seedlings will get by under a soda bottle. Shove the cut edge into the dirt and pile soil around it, or it'll likely end up in the neighbor's yard after the first windy night. Then check that no leaves press on the plastic.

Recent findings suggest that your jug's cap comes off, too. Sealed up, a jug warms fast on a sunny afternoon, and the seedling can overheat while you're still outside in a jacket. Lift the jugs off on mild, bright days and drop them back on at dusk. If you run short on jugs, reusable clear plastic bell cloches, like these Senwell cloches from Amazon, go on the same way. They come with metal ground stakes to keep them in place.

Bend flexible ½-inch (1.3 cm) PVC pipe or heavy wire into hoops about 4 feet (1.2 m) apart over a bed, then stretch frost fabric or clear greenhouse plastic across the top. One tunnel can shelter a whole raised bed or a long row of greens. A Haxnicks fleece tunnel from Walmart comes with the steel hoops already attached and stretches to about 10 feet (3 m).

So should it get fabric or plastic? Fabric is the low-fuss choice, since air moves through it and it can stay on for days. Plastic gets warmer in the daytime and sheds rain, but after dark it's no warmer than fabric. Closed plastic can cook the greens on a bright afternoon, so pull up a side or open the ends. Wet, heavy snow can flatten it, too. Snowy areas need sturdier hoops set closer together, plus a brush-off after each storm.

In a recent development, you can leave carrots, parsnips, and other root crops in the bed past fall. Heap straw or shredded leaves on the row, and many of them will keep until you want them. Soil under that pile doesn't freeze as deep or flip between frozen and thawed as often. Left in over winter, a parsnip is, honestly, a sweeter parsnip come spring. Dig the rest before they bolt.

Industry observers note that mulch only protects the soil, though – it won't keep exposed kale or chard leaves from freezing on a hard night, so pair it with a cover. Be picky about the straw, too. Hay and bargain bales can be full of weed seed. GardenStraw wheat straw mulch from Lowe's is filtered, with most of the seed screened out, in a 2-cubic-foot (57L) box.

Sources indicate that an old storm window in the garage is halfway to a cold frame. Hinge it to the back of a bottomless wooden box, or right onto a raised bed. Inside, it can run 10 to 20°F (6 to 11°C) warmer than the open garden. Spinach, mâche, and winter lettuce do well in one. Backyard Discovery's cedar cold frame from Walmart has a lid that lifts on its own once the inside passes 70°F (21°C).

Glass is heavy and can break, so secure the pane firmly so a gust can't slam it, and sand any sharp edges. Windows painted before 1978 may also contain lead paint – not something you want flaking into a food bed. On sunny days, heat is the bigger risk, so prop the lid open. Tuck a sensor like this AcuRite wireless thermometer from Lowe's inside the frame, and check it from the house.

Sources indicate that pots give you an option a bed doesn't. Their weak spot is down in the roots. Those are usually far less cold-hardy than the leaves, and a pot doesn't give them much soil for cover, so a freeze reaches them faster than roots in the ground. Still, you can pick up a pot of parsley, kale, or salad greens and carry it somewhere better. Crowd them by a wall the wind doesn't hit and throw burlap or bubble wrap around the bunch.

In a recent development, water them well the day before a hard freeze. Wet soil freezes more slowly than dry soil, it turns out. On the bitter nights, carry the smaller ones into an unheated garage or shed. Get them back out the next morning, or once that cold spell is over. Greens left in a dim garage for days can come out pale and leggy.

Industry observers note that kale, collards, spinach, parsley, and cabbage can take a lot. Frost under 28°F (-2°C) usually doesn't bother them, but when the forecast calls for low 20°s F (around -6°C), cover them anyway. Lettuce, Swiss chard, beets, and carrots aren't quite as tough. Damage can show up in the mid- to upper 20°s (about -4 to -2°C). Mâche is the odd one out among salad greens and holds up better than lettuce. Beans, peppers, and tomatoes can't take even a light frost.

Recent findings suggest that these ratings aren't fixed, though. Two varieties of the same crop can differ in hardiness, and an established kale plant usually gets through a freeze in better shape than one transplanted last week. Plants that have had several weeks of slowly cooling weather also hold up better than ones hit by a hard freeze after a warm spell. Watch how long the cold lasts, not just how low it'll go.

A greenhouse would be nice, sure, but straw over the carrots, fabric over the kale, and a couple of milk jugs over the late lettuce will carry a garden a long way. Keep a frost blanket folded by the back door. The night the forecast suddenly drops, it'll be the first thing you reach for.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success demonstrates that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that but it’s crucial to slow down a bit and figure out if that tree is...
  • Honestly, the messiest trees might promise the world, but they are sure to make your life infinitely more difficult, perhaps dropping spiky seed balls or spreading thousands of unwanted seedlings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most of us do not have unlimited free time to garden. That’s why terms like “easy-care” and “drought-tolerant” can make a shrub so appealing. And if the tree characterized as “easy-care” is also gorgeous, it has a good chance of finding its way into our garden.

Industry observers note that but it’s crucial to slow down a bit and figure out if that tree is... well, if it's messy. Messy trees can be easy enough to grow, but you may be signing yourself up for relentless cleanup – and some stunning ornamentals that light up your landscape may create far more work for you than you realize.

Honestly, the messiest trees might promise the world, but they are sure to make your life infinitely more difficult, perhaps dropping spiky seed balls or spreading thousands of unwanted seedlings. And garden stores know better than to stick a “messy” label on them.

Recent findings suggest that keen to swerve the cleanup? Well, Gardening Know How is here to help!

Recent findings suggest that we’ve identified six of the messiest trees around (none of which happen to be your birth month tree, thankfully) and we’re here to rat them out. We’ll outline the features of each that will win your heart, as well as what they do to earn their “messy” status, plus an equally beautiful, less messy alternative. You're welcome.

Ah the ginkgo. It’s hard to add this fabulous, ancient tree to the “messy” list given its incredible history; after all, its lineage dates back over 270 million years, and it is known as a “living fossil” because, for years, botanists believed that the tree was extinct. They found fossil evidence of its unique, fan-shaped leaves, but nary a living tree was found for years. Then, one day in the 1600s, a small grove was located in a temple garden in Japan and the world got ginkgos again.

These are wonderful, noble trees with leaves that blaze gold in the autumn. However, do not invite one into your landscape until you are assured that it is a male. Female ginkgos make the “messy” list because they drop oodles of fleshy, cherry-sized fruit that smell like rotting flesh when crushed. You’ll be cleaning up and holding your nose for a month.

According to recent reports, plant instead: a male gingko. There are cultivars that are all-male (like this beautiful Autumn Gold Ginkgo Tree from Nature Hills) and this is not the time to demand gender equality!

Eastern cottonwood is a messy tree with a lot to recommend it. It is a fast-growing, deciduous tree, large and impressive, sometimes reaching 150 ft tall. It plays a critical role in the ecosystem, supporting 249 caterpillar species (including your birth month caterpillar). It is also lovely, with flat leaf stems that catch even the lightest breeze, causing the heart-shaped leaves to shimmer and rustle.

It has been revealed that but look out below! Every year a female cottonwood produces a massive volume of tiny seeds wrapped in sticky white, cotton-like fibers that blanket lawns, clog gutters, and wrap around air conditioners.

Plant instead: the Chinese pistache. If you long for a large shade tree but want to avoid cottonwood's fluffy seeds, plant a Chinese pistache like this one from Brighter Blooms. It grows more slowly and fits in well in residential gardens.

According to recent reports, southern magnolias are the belles of the ball in the landscape, with their goblet-shaped, intensely fragrant white blooms and large, glossy leaves. The trees are evergreens that can grow above 60 feet (20m) tall and half that wide. They have a real presence in the garden.

But don’t fall for this pretty face until you learn of the work you will be required to do to keep your garden looking good. Southern magnolia trees shed, and they shed almost constantly. They shed their heavy waxy leaves; they shed their large seed cones; and they shed spent petals. Picking up in a year-round job.

Plant instead: flowering dogwood. If you love the Southern magnolia’s showy flowers, sub in a flowering dogwood (aka the tree quietly replacing magnolias everywhere). It is a more manageable size with lovely white “flowers” that are actually bracts.

A post shared by Vikram Baliga (@the.plant.prof).

The gorgeous cloud of white spring flowers has turned many a head, and the Bradford pear (despite the controversy surrounding it) is widely used as a street tree and even in gardens. It offers a graceful, symmetrical shape, pretty spring blossoms, and lively fall foliage.

However, best enjoy looking at this little flowering tree in someone else’s yard, because those white flowers that look like they were cultivated by angels actually smell awful! Some liken the odor to rotting fish, others to sweaty foot fungus. This happens when the tree is in full bloom, and the petals hold onto the smell as they fall.

Plant instead: a wild cherry (Prunus avium). Like the Bradford pear, a cherry erupts in clusters of stunning white flowers just as spring rolls in. But something like the Montmorency Cherry Tree from Nature Hills is a native and its blossoms smell like flowers instead of fish. Those flowers produce fruit that is loved by local birds.

Oh the autumn color you’ll enjoy with a sweetgum tree! This fast-growing native tree has lovely starry leaves that turn all sorts of fiery colors before they fall. Each leaf has five to seven lobes that turn orange, crimson, and purple in autumn. A sweetgum is a tolerant tree, accepting heat, drought, and soil compaction, as well as feeding birds in winter.

Recent findings suggest that but sweetgum has its downsides: primarily, the hard, spiky "gumballs" that hurt bare feet and make mowing difficult. Yes, this lovely tree drops thousands of woody seed pods from winter through spring. They hurt your feet if you walk barefoot, and even with shoes on, they can trip you up and cause ankle injuries. They even destroy lawnmower blades. Yet they are really difficult to rake up.

Plant instead: red maple (Acer rubrum). If you want a tree for fall color and shade, a seedless red maple cultivar will treat you right. It offers similar shade and a brilliant red or orange autumn display and similar shade.

According to recent reports, what a mix! Crabapples offer spectacular spring flowers and attractive berries. They are small trees, usually under 25 feet (8m) tall, grown for their ornamental beauty and wildlife value.

However, if you get a messy crabapple variety, you may come to regret inviting the tree into your landscape. The large, juicy fruits fall readily from the tree and make the ground below a slippery mess. Having to trudge through the slippery rotting fruits is icky and even dangerous, but cleaning up cannot be called fun wither.

Recent findings suggest that plant instead: a “clean” variety of crabapple. You can select a fruitless variety like Spring Snow Crabapple (Malus 'Spring Snow'), with dense clusters of fragrant, pure white blossoms in mid-spring. Or, if you prefer, a Prairifire Flowering Crabapple Tree from Nature Hills, which promises to be far too tempting to local birds to ever spill a berry.

Of course, if you have the time to do the cleanup, then there's no harm planting a messy tree in your yard. Just be sure you're willing to roll your sleeves up and get cracking when things get mucky – and if not, one of our beautiful alternatives is definitely the better choice for you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I know, I know; poinsettias are absolutely the traditional choice for festive decorating, but there's another festive container plant that deserves a place by your front door this winter.

One of those underrated beauties that deserves its time in the spotlight, this holiday plant may not have the bold and colorful bracts of a classic poinsettia, but what it lacks in showy flowers, it more than makes up for in fragrance, evergreen foliage and year-round appeal.

In fact, if you're looking for a festive container plant that keeps on giving long after the holiday decorations have come down, it could be just the thing you're looking for (and then some!).

In a recent development, poinsettias are practically synonymous with the holidays, and little wonder; their bright red, pink or white foliage brings an instant splash of festive color. Still, there's no getting away from the fact that their appeal is largely seasonal. They're tender plants, usually grown indoors in the US, and need warmth, bright indirect light, careful watering, and lots of TLC to keep them looking their best.

Recent findings suggest that once the holidays are over and those colorful bracts begin to fade, many poinsettias end up in the compost or trash. And, while it's possible to keep them growing and even encourage them to develop their colorful bracts again the following year, doing so takes a little effort.

Enter stage left, then, the beautiful sweet box (Sarcococca).

Obviously, sweet box offers a rather different proposition, as this handsome evergreen shrub doesn't have to be replaced when Christmas is over. In fact, its glossy leaves provide structure and greenery throughout the year, while its winter flowers bring a welcome surprise just when the garden can feel at its dullest.

Recent findings suggest that and it's not just about looks, either! Sweet box has a secret weapon that poinsettias simply can't compete with: its extraordinary perfume.

That's right, folks; sweet box produces masses of creamy-white flowers in winter, often tucked discreetly beneath its glossy leaves. They might not look particularly impressive from a distance, but get close and you'll discover why this shrub is so treasured, as they release a perfume often described as a combination of vanilla and jasmine.

Recent findings suggest that it's surprisingly powerful for such delicate blooms, and on a still winter day, the scent can drift through the garden and greet you as you approach your front door. Especially if you opt for a variety like the Sweet & Lo™ Sweet Box from Proven Winners.

Once flowering finishes, sweet box can produce ornamental berries, which mature from red to dark purple or black depending on the species and variety. And it does all of this while standing in partial or full shade, no less!

Although some sweet box varieties can eventually become quite substantial shrubs, its slow-growing nature also makes it a useful long-term container plant. (You won't be constantly battling to keep it in shape, for starters, although a light trim after flowering can help maintain a neat outline if needed).

Just be sure to choose a pot with drainage holes and use a good moisture-retentive potting mix. Pop it somewhere sheltered in partial or full shade, and water when the compost begins to dry – just like all container-grown plants, it will need a little more attention to watering than those growing in the ground, particularly during dry spells.

In a recent development, of course, there's nothing wrong with a beautiful poinsettia, but if you'd rather invest in a plant that offers more than a few weeks of seasonal color, sweet box is well worth your time... not to mention a place in your heart. Not least of all because it's the sort of hard-working hero plant that continues to provide beauty long after the festive season has passed.

Industry observers note that if your home and garden is full of those awkward shady spots where other plants might struggle, then, look no further! And if not? Well, still show it some love, I say – for a festive container with fragrance, character and staying power, sweet box is a very hard plant to beat.

Maryland Man Convicted of $18.7 Million Medicare Fraud for Respiratory Testing Scheme Targeting Nursing Homes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.
  • Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable.
  • Industry observers note that “This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.

Sources indicate that “Mr. Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable. This verdict reinforces our message: there is nowhere to hide for those who commit fraud. We will find you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law,” said U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes for the District of Maryland. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office, along with our law-enforcement partners, remains committed to rooting out fraud and holding accountable those who exploit our vulnerable victims and who steal our taxpayer money.”.

Industry observers note that “This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul. “Patrick Britton-Harr will now face the consequences of his greed and brazen crimes. In addition to this healthcare fraud scheme, Britton-Harr was previously convicted for investment fraud in which the FBI uncovered a separate scheme where he defrauded private citizens. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will not rest until fraudsters like Mr. Britton Harr are brought to justice.”.

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Patrick Britton-Harr, 42, of Annapolis, offered COVID-19 tests to nursing homes across the country in 2020 when these facilities were desperate for COVID-19 testing services. After specimens were collected from nursing home residents and other laboratories performed COVID-19 testing, Britton-Harr billed Medicare for separate, high-priced respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests purportedly conducted in a laboratory he owned in Arizona. Britton-Harr falsely claimed to Medicare that treating physicians ordered these extensive RPP tests, which screened for more than 30 respiratory pathogens. In reality, physicians never ordered the tests for their nursing home patients, and several physicians testified at trial they had never ordered an RPP test for any patient during the entirety of their medical careers.

Through his company, Provista Health, Britton-Harr fraudulently billed Medicare $18.7 million for RPP testing purportedly performed in just six months, of which Medicare paid more than $7.2 million. Evidence at trial demonstrated how Britton-Harr exploited inexperienced employees, including a family member and high school and college aged interns, by directing them to bill Medicare for an RPP test every time a COVID-19 test was performed. Britton-Harr further directed the billing of RPP tests supposedly performed at his Arizona laboratory after he had already closed the laboratory, barred staff from working in the laboratory, and no longer had the equipment necessary to run RPP tests. Additional evidence at trial proved that Britton-Harr billed Medicare for RPP tests that were never performed, including billing for tests for nursing home residents who were already deceased.

Britton-Harr used the proceeds of his fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, purchasing, among other things, a $112,500 Porsche 911, and making $25,000 monthly mortgage payments on his Annapolis waterfront mansion.

The jury convicted Britton-Harr of five counts of health care fraud and one count of transactional money laundering. Britton-Harr faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison for each count. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled at a later date. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

HHS-OIG and FBI investigated the case.

Trial Attorney Chris Wenger of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Ari Evans for the District of Maryland are prosecuting the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

In a recent development, the Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, at the moment comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

Fall-planted bulbs that flower in spring are surely the easiest, cheapest way to add color to your garden. Pop the bulbs into the ground in fall, then do absolutely nothing at all until green stems pierce the cold spring soil to light up your yard with fabulous flowers. From tulips to crocus, hyacinths to Dutch iris, there are plenty of showstopper bulbs you can still plant in November. As long as your ground isn’t frozen or waterlogged, all these beauties can be planted now, at a depth that's three times the bulb's height. If you live in a colder USDA zone and already past your first frost date, simply plant bulbs in a container in a sheltered spot instead.

When you’re planting bulbs in late fall, the secret to success is great drainage so they root rather than rot. That’s easily done by giving bulbs an inch-deep layer of grit to sit on at the base of the planting hole. You could fork out on horticultural grit, or you could simply use good ol’ poultry grit made of crushed granite like CZ Grain Chicken Grit, available from Walmart. You may need to protect tasty tulip bulbs from hungry squirrels, but then you can leave the rest to Mother Nature.

Sources indicate that if it’s a while since you went bulb shopping, you’re in for a lovely surprise because plant breeders have been busy creating all sorts of wonderful fresh flower shapes and color combinations. From double-petalled tulips that look just like peonies to fragrant hyacinths in dramatic hues, these backyard blooms are a real springtime treat and planting them should be on everyone's list of gardening jobs in November. So let's skip straight to the good bit, shall we? Here’s my pick of dazzling spring-flowering bulbs to plant in late fall. Get the drainage right and all these will return year in, year out and with prices from 35 cents a bulb, there’s an option to suit every budget.
