📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Evergreens are often dismissed as quiet, supporting background players in the garden: solid green shrubs tucked along foundations while flamboyant perennials hog the limelight.
  • According to recent reports, growing real evergreen plants in containers can provide a brilliant Christmas display that continues looking attractive all winter.
  • Industry observers note that best of all, these container-friendly evergreens transition seamlessly from Christmas décor to winter curb appeal that lasts long after the holiday lights come down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Evergreens are often dismissed as quiet, supporting background players in the garden: solid green shrubs tucked along foundations while flamboyant perennials hog the limelight. Yet when chosen thoughtfully, they can become show-stopping centerpieces. This is a time of year to celebrate the holiday season, but rather than relying on temporary displays, why not go for something with real staying power?

According to recent reports, growing real evergreen plants in containers can provide a brilliant Christmas display that continues looking attractive all winter. Flanking a front door or framing porch steps with holiday porch pots filled with living potted evergreens offers charm and longevity. Beyond classic deep emerald needles, today’s best container evergreens can deliver winter berries, flowers, contrasting textures, and even fragrance to greet guests as they arrive at your stoop.

Industry observers note that best of all, these container-friendly evergreens transition seamlessly from Christmas décor to winter curb appeal that lasts long after the holiday lights come down. With minimal upkeep, they lend easy elegance through the dark days of winter, then you can move them as needed to assist in decades-long displays. From trailing options to compact shrubs, here are 8 gorgeous evergreens you can use to transform your front porch into an enchanting holiday welcome.

Growing evergreens in containers unlocks wonderful design flexibility, allowing you to cluster different heights, trailing textures, and berry accents right at eye level near your doorway. However, while container-grown evergreens are generally easygoing and make great seasonal décor, they need a little more winter care than evergreens growing in the ground.

Because their potted roots sit above ground, they are more vulnerable to freezing temperatures and drying winter winds. It’s a good idea to choose evergreen varieties that are rated at least one or two USDA hardiness zones colder than your local climate, so plant roots have the best shot at surviving winter freezes unscathed.

Use frost-proof containers crafted from thick resin, fiberglass, glazed stoneware, or heavy wood. Avoid unglazed thin terracotta in cold climates, as trapped moisture will expand and crack clay walls. If your winters are very cold, consider wrapping the pots in burlap. Always leave unobstructed drainage holes and elevate your pots slightly on pot feet so icy water doesn't have a chance to pool underneath. You can buy Tortoise Pot Toes from Amazon to help ensure the best drainage.

Fill the containers with a coarse, fast-draining potting mix. Once you are past the holiday season and heading to spring, you can add a slow-release organic fertilizer. Even in winter, evergreens continue losing moisture through their foliage. Check the soil every couple of weeks and water deeply whenever the top two inches (5cm) feel dry and temperatures are above freezing. You’re now ready to add some of these evergreens to make your porch sparkle during Christmas and shine all winter long….

Alberta spruce is a classic choice for a Christmas tree, but most are large. If you fancy flanking your front door with classic, miniature Christmas trees, dwarf Alberta spruce (Picea glauca ‘Conica’) is perfect for a pot. Hardy across zones 3-8, this conifer naturally grows into a dense, velvety green, symmetrical cone, so it requires zero shearing to maintain its crisp silhouette. Also, because it adds just 2-4 inches (5-10cm) of growth per year, it thrives in a generous 14-18-inch (35-45cm) container for years, before needing upsizing or transplanting into the yard.

According to recent reports, place in full sun to light afternoon shade, rotating every few weeks. Keep the potting mix evenly moist but sharply drained, and mist occasionally. For a little extra holiday magic, underplant with trailing wintergreen or variegated ivy. Avoid heavy ornaments that might bend the fine branch tips. You can buy Dwarf Alberta Spruce from Nature Hills at a 30% discount. Add a couple for a lovely, symmetrical entryway feature.

Boxwood (Buxus spp.) brings classic English-garden elegance to winter porches in zones 5-9. Its dense clusters of small, glossy leaves stay green through sub-freezing weather. For containers, choose compact, cold-hardy cultivars such as Green Velvet (which forms a lush, rounded mound) or Green Gem. You can buy Brighter Blooms Green Velvet Boxwood from Walmart. Alternatively, go for pre-trained pyramid and globe topiaries for instant architectural polish.

Place potted boxwoods in partial shade to full sun. In northern zones, shelter them from harsh afternoon winter sun and drying winds. Plant in well-drained potting soil, and water deeply when unfrozen soil dries out. Dress for the holidays with velvet ribbon bows or tuck crimson winterberry stems into the soil around the base. Save any light shaping shears for late spring after the risk of last frost is passed.

Nothing announces the arrival of Christmas quite like holly (Ilex spp.), with its glossy leaves and scarlet berries. While towering tree hollies promptly outgrow porch pots, compact shrub cultivars thrive in containers in zones 5-9. Look for dwarf selections such as Little Red or compact Japanese Helleri. Alternatively, try deciduous winterberry Berry Poppins. Buy Proven Winners Berry Poppins Winterberry Holly from Plant Addicts for a container-sized beauty loaded with vibrant berry clusters.

It has been revealed that just remember that hollies are dioecious. To enjoy berries, you need a female cultivar paired near a compatible male (such as Mr Poppins for winterberry). Failing that, buy a nursery pot where both sexes are planted together. Grow hollies in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic potting mix. Keep berries safely out of reach of pets, and enjoy watching winter songbirds visit as spring approaches.

Industry observers note that if your front porch sits beneath a deep overhang or faces north where sun-loving conifers struggle, Japanese skimmia (Skimmia japonica) is a revelation. Hardy in zones 6-8, this neat, mounded broadleaf evergreen thrives in partial to full shade, retaining leathery, aromatic leaves all year. Better still, it delivers multi-season magic: in fall and early winter, male cultivars like Rubella produce clusters of flower buds that last right through Christmas, before opening into fragrant spring blossoms, while female varieties like Reevesiana bear true red berries.

According to recent reports, plant skimmia in an acidic, humus-rich potting mix (such as an ericaceous blend) with sharp drainage. Water regularly during dry spells, using rainwater if your tap water is hard. Nestle pots in a sheltered porch corner that is protected from icy gales. You can buy Skimmia Male Plants from Plant Addicts for shade-loving beauty to bedazzle on a covered porch. Add pinecones and ribbons to make pots festive.

Also known as eastern teaberry or boxberry, American wintergreen (Gaultheria procumbens) is a low-growing native evergreen groundcover. But it punches above its compact 6-inch (15cm) height in winter containers. Hardy in zones 3-8, its shiny, oval leaves transform over winter, from deep green to mahogany-bronze in cold weather. This provides a gorgeous backdrop for large, glossy red berries that cling to the stems all winter long.

Because it trails gracefully over pot rims, it makes a lovely festive spiller around the base of dwarf spruce, boxwood, or winterberry stems in mixed holiday planters. Give it a spot in partial to full shade. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic potting soil. Keep soil consistently damp and avoid lime-heavy fertilizers. You can buy Arbor Day Foundation Store’s Wintergreen Teaberry Pot Plants from Amazon in triple packs. Perfect under a porch cover, awning, or larger tree or shrub.

Goldcrest cypress aka Goldcrest Monterey cypress (Hesperocyparis macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’) is also sold as lemon cypress, and it lives up to its names in winter porches. Hardy in zones 7-10 (and also enjoyed as a cool-room or sheltered patio container specimen in colder zones), this upright conifer is filled with chartreuse-gold foliage that releases a zesty aroma when you brush past it. You can buy Wonderland Flora’s Lemon Cypress Goldcrest Wilma Plants from Walmart in packs of four.

Industry observers note that its narrow, columnar shape fits neatly into tight entryway corners and pairs symmetrically beside front doors. Grow Goldcrest in full sun to intensify its golden hues, and plant in a fast-draining potting mix. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, but don’t let roots sit in soggy saucers. Dress the pot base with pinecones and burgundy ribbon for a contemporary holiday look that keeps sparkling into spring.

If you need to soften the edges of a structured winter pot, add some cascading English ivy (Hedera helix). Hardy in zones 4-9, this classic vining evergreen offers lobed emerald or crisp cream-and-gold variegations. Try cultivars like Glacier and Goldchild to brighten shady entryways with ease. While it can be invasive in the ground, it thrives in containers. Plant around the lip of mixed planters with upright boxwood or red-berried skimmia, or train up a wire obelisk for vertical interest.

Recent findings suggest that ivy thrives in partial to full shade, and prefers slightly drier, well-drained potting soil. Overwatering in winter is the main enemy. Just snip stray runners occasionally to keep trails tidy, and never allow stems to root into surrounding masonry. You can buy Glacier Ivy from Plant Addicts for trailing creams and greens to add lush, lively winter movement.

If you want guests to pause in delight at your front door, plant sweet box (Sarcococca confusa). Hardy in zones 6-9, this understated, slow-growing broadleaf evergreen features dense, pointed leaves that look refined all year. What makes it unique for holiday decorating is that it flowers in winter. Depending on where you garden, you’ll have either buds or open flowers on this evergreen shrub at Christmas time. As a bonus, these creamy flowers are sweetly fragrant even on chilly days.

Industry observers note that sweet box thrives in deep to partial shade and prefers shelter from winds, so a covered front porch or courtyard alcove is ideal. Plant in a medium-sized container filled with rich, well-drained, neutral-to-slightly-acidic potting mix. Keep soil evenly moist when unfrozen. Minimal pruning is required: simply snip a few fragrant sprigs to tuck into holiday vases. You can buy Hirt’s Gardens Sweet & Lo Sweet Box Plants from Amazon for a shade-loving evergreen that fills entryways with honey scent.

It has been revealed that picture a hose still screwed onto the spigot in December. The water behind it has nowhere to go. Once nights stay below 32°F (0°C), it can freeze solid, and copper and brass don't have much give. Something splits. That repair bill usually runs well past what the faucet cost, so it pays to sort out how to winterize an outdoor faucet now.

It's a fall chore, best done the same day you winterize sprinklers. The annoying part is where the damage hides. From the yard, the faucet can look fine while the pipe behind it has cracked a few inches inside the wall. Nobody sees that until the water's back on.

Recent findings suggest that outdoor faucet winterization is mostly about getting water out and keeping it from getting trapped again. Take off the hose, shut off the supply, drain what's left, and add a cover for backup. Try to finish alongside your other gardening winterizing tasks, and before the first hard freeze indicates up in the forecast.

If you only get to one step today, make it this one. Any hose left on the spigot holds water inside the faucet, and that goes for frost-free models too – the water has nowhere to drain while the hose is attached. Splitters, watering timers, and quick-connect fittings trap water the same way, so pull them all off.

Then empty the hose. Stretch it down a slope or drape loops over a fence rail so the water runs out both ends. Leftover water can freeze and split it, and a drained hose stored out of the weather generally holds up longer. Suncast's 100-foot Hose Hideaway from Walmart keeps a coiled hose off the ground under a lid.

It has been revealed that start inside. Standard faucets usually have their own shutoff, somewhere close to where the pipe goes out through the wall, often in a basement, crawl space, or utility room. Look up between the ceiling joists, too. A round handle turns clockwise until it stops. If it's a lever, a quarter turn puts it crosswise to the pipe, and that's closed.

Recent findings suggest that not every home has one, and older houses often don't, which makes it harder to winterize hose bib lines without shutting off water to the whole house. If you're not sure what an unlabeled valve is, leave it alone. Close the wrong one, and it's no fun to find out halfway through washing dishes. Frost-free faucets, like this SharkBite one, work differently and may not need this step.

According to recent reports, for faucets without a dedicated indoor shutoff, a Freeze Miser outdoor faucet protector offers another option. It screws onto the spigot and automatically releases a small amount of water when the water temperature drops below 37°F (3°C), helping prevent freezing. Unlike conventional winterizing, this method requires leaving the water supply on and the outdoor faucet fully open.

Head back outside and open the faucet all the way. Some water should run out, slow to a trickle, and stop. Did it keep flowing? Then the indoor valve isn't closed all the way, or it's not the right valve at all.

In a recent development, some shutoffs have a little cap on the side, called a bleeder. Leave the outdoor faucet open so air can get in, set a bucket underneath, and back the cap off slowly. Water will dribble out. When it quits, screw the cap back on. Many plumbers will leave the outdoor faucet open all winter. Some valve makers say to close it, though, so go by whatever came with yours.

An outdoor faucet cover holds in a little of the warmth that seeps through the wall from inside. The rigid type (like the image above) is a foam-lined dome with a cord that pulls it snug against the siding. Home Depot's Everbilt hard outdoor faucet cover is a good cheap option. Flexible pouches go on more like a sock (see image below), and the Thinsulate-lined faucet socks on Amazon come two to a pack.

Either kind should sit flat against the wall with no gap for cold air. Check it after windy nights, because covers do get knocked loose. It's backup, not a substitute for unhooking hoses and draining the line, and outdoor spigot winter protection still starts with an empty faucet. An Ambient Weather Wi-Fi weather station can send temperature alerts to your phone before a hard freeze.

Sources indicate that plenty of people hear frost-free and figure that means forget about it. That's about half right, maybe. From the yard, a frost-free outdoor faucet looks like any other spigot. Its handle turns a long stem, and the part that stops the water sits way back at the end of it, where it's warmer. Close it, and the water in that stem should run out the spout. That only works if the faucet slopes a little toward the outside.

Industry observers note that so the hose still comes off, or water stays put and can freeze inside the wall, often unnoticed until spring. Damage, a level installation, or a pipe running through an unheated crawl space can leave one vulnerable too.

Correctly installed ones usually don't need the supply shut off and drained, but the manufacturer's instructions get the final say. Homes without an indoor shutoff can have a plumber fit a replacement such as the SharkBite one mentioned above.

If the faucet won't run or ice has formed around the spout, skip the torch, even if one happens to be sitting right there in the garage. No open flame, and nothing else that blasts heat at it, either. There's framing and insulation right behind that siding. Hair dryers are slower. Point it at the faucet and the wall around it and give it time. Keep the cord out of puddles.

Suspect a leak? Shut off the water to that line, or the main valve if there's no separate one, and call a plumber. Frozen pipe damage isn't always visible right away. A crack of ⅛ inch (3 mm) can let out up to 250 gallons (946L) a day, and it may not drip at all until the ice thaws or the water goes back on.

Industry observers note that most of what it takes to protect outdoor faucets from freezing – and to prevent frozen pipes behind them – is getting the water out and keeping it out. Get that done before the first hard frost, and the faucet should be ready come spring, with dry walls behind it.

S.M.A.R.T. stands for Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today, and for Julie Kelley, founder and manager of this international animal welfare organization, that means working towards global animal welfare, sharing essential information and facts about animals worldwide, and helping people understand the benefits that come from treating animals with compassion and care.

According to recent reports, letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

Industry observers note that in Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

The creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

According to recent reports, our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:.

Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source.

Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity.

Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety.

Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior.

NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership.

For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

Recent findings suggest that we created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. We could not function without the help of our amazing Volunteers.

Industry observers note that we successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

It has been revealed that we receive multiple enquiries from tourists who have found a cat or kitten, and they want to take it home with them to their country. Many times they have cared for them during their stay, provided medicine, bottle-fed babies, etc. This has become increasingly common, with visitors seeing cats all over Greece. Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

In a recent development, you can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your new pet to travel home with you. Or we can foster a cat you rescue while you are in Greece and deal with the veterinary needs, papers etc. The cat can travel after you leave with a flight buddy or one of our volunteers.

What better souvenir to have from Greece than a beautiful cat that needed special love and care?

Sources indicate that everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

In a recent development, we would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Working together is the future. We are also collaborating with some officials regarding some policies involving the strays and to help create some standards for housing the strays. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

Sources indicate that A rather significant goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. This is a tall order, but we are looking for someone who would like to leave a legacy.

We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

Our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

Some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

Cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

It has been revealed that volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

Industry observers note that people can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

Recent findings suggest that if youâre visiting Greece and see a lot of stray cats, itâs a good idea to ask around if there is a local organization helping to take care of them. If you see an injured cat, you should immediately try to find a responsible person or contact the local police.

You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.

Forty-eight dogs â mostly French Bulldogs and English Bulldogs â found in what authorities are describing as a clandestine breeding operation in San Juan de Miraflores, Peru.

And when you read what was found, it is hard not to feel angry.

Authorities discovered the animals in appalling conditions on September 28 in an apartment on JirÃ³n Santiago RodrÃ­guez. The group included 25 French Bulldogs, nine English Bulldogs, eight mixed-breed dogs, five French Bulldog puppies, and one Dachshund. There was also a rooster. Local French Bulldog club, Club Frenchie, heard about the rescue through social media and immediately reached out to offer assistance. One member of the club spoke to a reporter from the Peruvian newspaper El Comercio about what they had witnessed:.

Sources indicate that âThe state of health was absolutely deplorable. There were dogs covered in feces, filthy, with no hygiene whatsoever, dogs with broken nails, bitten ears, and other serious problems,â he noted.

The dogs were brought to the Municipal Veterinary Clinic in San Juan de Miraflores, where they were examined and received treatment for a range of conditions. Most were suffering from heat stress, and many had excessively long nails, some bleeding, skin problems, fungal challenges, eye infections, surgical scars, and other conditions requiring medical attention. Six puppies reportedly needed incubator care, with two described as being in a particularly fragile condition.

Following the intervention, the animals were taken to the municipal veterinary service, and some have since been moved into foster care. The San Juan de Miraflores Provincial Corporate Criminal Prosecutor's Office is investigating the case, and FÃ©lix Sonco and Darlys Vanegas were arrested at the scene.

As if the horrendous conditions that greeted rescuers werenât disturbing enough, it appears that this wasnât simply a breeding operation, but an illegal, makeshift veterinary clinic.

Some of these dogs had undergone surgery on their vocal cords; a barbaric procedure known as debarking. Being kept in cramped and filthy conditions meant that these dogs were barking and crying constantly. Debarking was a way to reduce noise and avoid complaints.

It has been revealed that they didnât improve conditions. They didnât provide relief. They simply removed their ability to voice their distress.

Sources indicate that evidence also suggests that several female Bulldogs were bred repeatedly, with some reportedly forced to carry as many as ten litters of puppies. Veterinary examination also found evidence that crude cesarean surgeries had been performed prematurely to get puppies out faster and back on the market, while the mothers, if they survived, were bred again.

Investigators reportedly found premature newborn puppies inside an unsterilized incubator, while puppies were being sold for around 1,500 to 2,500 Peruvian soles each â roughly $400 to $670 USD.

French Bulldogs and English Bulldogs are brachycephalic breeds. Their shortened skull and squishy faces are a substantial part of their appeal. But there is a very uncomfortable truth behind that cute face.

That same anatomy that many people find irresistible can make it harder for a dog to breathe, exercise, sleep, regulate their body temperature, and, in some cases, give birth.

We have to stop pretending these things are simply âpart of being a Bulldog.â.

A dog struggling to breathe is not just a snorer. A dog that overheats easily is not just âsensitive to the heat.â These are medical problems.

Brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome (BOAS) refers to the conditions that affect breeds with a shortened skull, or âbrachycephaly.â These conditions include hypoplastic trachea (narrow  windpipe), stenotic nares (narrow nostrils), and a tongue and soft palate that are too large and long for the mouth, resulting in obstruction of the airways and difficulty swallowing.

These issues have led many veterinary professionals and animal welfare advocates to question the ethics of breeding these dogs. When a physical characteristic can affect basic functions like breathing and temperature regulation, choosing which dogs reproduce needs to consider more than appearance.

Sources indicate that that little flat face. Those big eyes. The stout little body. The funny little snorts.

Most people see cute, even adorable. But as veterinarians, we see a whole list of problems that need to be monitored.

A Bulldog can be an absolutely wonderful companion and still have anatomy that puts them at risk for serious health problems. Breeding of these dogs should require more responsibility, not less, with breeders selecting for less extreme conformations.

In a recent development, there is something very sad about how much importance we place on how dogs look. A certain face. A certain size. A certain coat. A certain breed.

The more desirable that look becomes, the more money there is in producing it. That creates a market, and unfortunately, where there is money, there will always be those willing to cut corners.

It has been revealed that this does not mean that every breeder is bad. There are responsible breeders who health-test their dogs, carefully select breeding pairs, provide appropriate veterinary care, and take responsibility for the puppies they bring into the world. Those who are actively trying to breed healthier versions of dogs whose health and function have been crippled through selective breeding for exaggerated features.

Puppy mills are something very different.

The problem is when the animals producing those puppies become a means to an end.

A female dog becomes a breeding machine.

And veterinary care becomes an expense to minimize or avoid, not an essential part of responsible animal care.

It has been revealed that when it comes to looking for your next four-legged family member, start your search at an animal shelter. Research your favorite breed and know how to recognize a suspicious situation.

If you are planning to purchase or adopt a puppy, you should be able to inspect the home or facility where the puppy was raised, and meet the puppyâs mother. Breeders who are unwilling or unable to allow this raise suspicions of unethical practice, and if you are concerned about a potential welfare issue, donât be tempted to buy a puppy to ârescueâ it â this simply finances the operation. Instead, contact your local animal control agency, humane society, sheriff, or police department.

Industry observers note that when extreme conformation interferes with breathing and thermoregulation, when it increases the risk of difficult births and chronic airway problems, we need to consider whether breeding these dogs is the right thing to do. But if people will buy them, people will breed them.

Itâs up to us to look past the adorable face we saw on Instagram and ask:.

Are they breathing comfortably?

Do they have functional airways?

Poinsettias might be the traditional choice for festive decorating, but they're not the only Christmas houseplants capable of bringing a splash of holiday color indoors.

Recent findings suggest that if you're looking for something a little different this year, there is a holiday plant that promises the same bold red hues of a poinsettia, along with glossy succulent leaves and a surprisingly easygoing nature. And no, we're not talking about sweet box (although that's also a brilliant container plant to add to your shopping list).

Instead, we're dragging the beautiful Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) into the spotlight, as its flowers can last for weeks, making it a lovely way to brighten your home through the darker months.

Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

Often sold as a seasonal flowering plant, Flaming Katy is actually a tender perennial succulent, which means you don't necessarily have to throw it away once Christmas is over. In fact, all you have to do is give it the right conditions and it can continue growing for years, potentially rewarding you with another spectacular display.

There's no denying that poinsettias look impressive, but they can be surprisingly fussy about their surroundings, as they dislike cold draughts and sudden temperature changes – so much so that their leaves can drop. Overwatering is another common problem, particularly when plants are left sitting in decorative pots without adequate drainage.

Flaming Katy offers a much easier alternative, as its leaves store water, helping it cope with occasional dry spells, while its clusters of brightly colored flowers provide plenty of festive impact. Red is a particularly popular choice for Christmas, of course, although you can also find varieties with pink, orange, yellow and white flowers, too.

In a recent development, better still? Rather than providing a brief burst of colour, a healthy plant can remain in bloom for several weeks, sometimes even longer depending on the variety and growing conditions.

Recent findings suggest that unlike some Christmas houseplants, this one doesn't need constant attention to keep looking good. Once you find a suitable position (a birght windowsill is ideal), the main thing is to avoid overwatering and make sure it receives enough light.

In a recent development, it also prefers average indoor humidity, so there's no need to mist it or create a particularly humid environment; in fact, good air circulation is more useful than excessive moisture around the leaves. Just keep it somewhere warm, ideally with temperatures around 60–75°F (16–24°C), and give it plenty of bright, indirect light (and remember that some gentle morning sunshine is generally welcome, too).

During the flowering period, you can remove individual faded flower clusters to keep the plant looking tidy, but there's no need for complicated pruning or constant feeding.

According to recent reports, perhaps the best thing about Flaming Katy is that, even though it's a Christmas houseplant, it doesn't have to be a disposable festive decoration; once flowering finishes, you can continue growing it as a foliage houseplant. With the right care, it can produce new growth and flower again.

Oh sure, poinsettias will always have their place in Christmas decorating, but Flaming Katy makes a convincing alternative if you'd prefer something colorful, undemanding and potentially longer-lasting when it comes to brightening up a home during winter. And unlike a certain fussy red plant that pops up everywhere in the holidays, this little flowering succulent really can stick around for years.

According to recent reports, hey, a festive purchase that really does keep on giving? Consider us sold!

What Your Jade Plant Needs in November – 5 Easy Ways to Unlock Lush Growth and Good Fortune in the New Year

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that with its sculptural trunk, plump leaves, and reputation as a symbol of prosperity and good fortune, a healthy jade plant (Crassula ovata) can thrive for decades.
  • Shorter days mean weaker sunlight streaming through the glass, while central heating inevitably clicks on.
  • Luckily, protecting your jade now is oh-so-simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that with its sculptural trunk, plump leaves, and reputation as a symbol of prosperity and good fortune, a healthy jade plant (Crassula ovata) can thrive for decades. Yet as November settles in, these plants quietly shift into semi-dormancy as less sun naturally fills the space. This can make a jade feel vulnerable if your care routine stays stuck in summer mode.

Shorter days mean weaker sunlight streaming through the glass, while central heating inevitably clicks on. Stand beside a sunny windowsill in the afternoon and it can feel cozy, yet by evening an icy chill radiates off the pane. Because of this, your jade plant care routine needs to adapt. It would be foolish to water as you did months earlier, or leave a prized specimen pressed against a drafty sill. If you’re not careful, you might risk triggering leaf drop, soft stems, or weak and leggy growth.

Luckily, protecting your jade now is oh-so-simple. Just a few seasonal adjustments prevent calamity, so you can preserve those glossy, coin-shaped leaves, and even encourage delicate star-shaped winter blooms. And for anyone looking to boost their fortunes in the latest year, it all starts here and now by giving your beloved jade plants the right care and attention. Here’s how to help yours thrive through winter, so it sees in spring in the very best shape.

Industry observers note that jade plant care this month comes down to balancing your own comfort against your plant’s natural seasonal rhythm. While you turn up the thermostat and pull the curtains against the dark, your jade craves bright, crisp days, cool nights, and dry feet. Even innocently shifting a pot aside to make room for holiday decor can plunge your sun-loving succulent into stressful gloom or into the path of a radiator blast.

Your local climate and USDA hardiness zone still shape indoor care. In northern regions (zones 3-6), dry furnace air and frosty windowpanes pose the biggest threats. In mild coastal or southern regions (zones 9-11), anyone who risks keeping jades outdoors on patios must watch for cool rainstorms that might waterlog pots.

In a recent development, before starting your tasks, clear any dust off the leaves with a soft brush so they absorb maximum winter light. If you fancy a closer look at your jade plant’s nooks and crannies, invest in a magnifying glass or a loupe, like the JarLink 30X 60X Illuminated Jeweler’s Loupe, available on Amazon. This can help you spot early mealybug fluff or scale bumps. It’s also a good idea to verify that drainage holes aren't blocked, before you start these essential jade care tasks.

Scaling back your watering routine is the single most impactful step you can take for a jade plant in November. As daylight dwindles and growth slows to a crawl, jade roots absorb moisture more slowly than they did in summer. Leaving roots sitting in a damp potting mix for weeks at a time invites fungal root rot. Before reaching for the watering can, push your index finger 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) down into the soil, insert a plain wooden chopstick to the bottom. Alternatively, use a probe like the inexpensive XLUX Plant Soil Moisture Meter from Amazon.

Industry observers note that if any dampness or dark soil clings to it, wait another week. When the mix is dry, water thoroughly until excess drains out the bottom hole. Empty the saucer immediately. Keep plant age and variety in mind. Compact varieties like Hobbit and Gollum, or young plants in small 4-inch (10cm) pots, dry out faster than massive specimens in deep tubs. Avoid over-correcting: if lower leaves feel thin, soft, or wrinkled, your jade plant is ready for a drink.

According to recent reports, by November, the sun sits lower in the sky and a jade that did fine in an east or west window all summer may only catch a sliver of the light it needs now. Jade plants require at least 4-6 hours of bright, direct light daily to keep stems sturdy and leaves compact. This is especially true of variegated cultivars like Tricolor or Variegata, which have less chlorophyll and lose their creamy-pink margins in dim rooms. Relocate your jade to an unobstructed south-facing window or a bright west-facing sill. Make the move gradually over 3-4 days so leaves do not scorch.

Watch for early signs of light starvation, such as pale new leaves or elongated stems with wide gaps between leaf pairs (known as etiolation). If natural winter light falls short in northern latitudes, supplement with a full-spectrum LED grow bulb positioned 12-18 inches (30-45cm) above the canopy for 10-12 hours daily. Feit Electric's 9-Watt BR30 Medium E26 Full-Spectrum LED Grow Light Bulb from The Home Depot will screw into a plain old lamp socket. Switch your grow lights off at night, though. Uninterrupted dark, cool nights trigger mature jades to set flower buds.

Put your palm on the window glass one of these chilly mornings, and you'll know why the sill can be a rough spot. Jade has zero tolerance for frost or abrupt temperature shifts. Leaves pressed against a freezing pane can get damaged even indoors. Pull your potted jade back 3-6 inches (8-15cm) from cold windowpanes, and slide a piece of insulating cork or folded cloth beneath the pot on chilly stone or marble sills.

Also keep jades clear of exterior entry doors that blast icy air every time someone walks in, as well as radiators and heaters: neither extreme is a good neighbor for a jade, really. Aim for steady daytime temperatures between 60-75°F (16-24°C) and nights around 50-55°F (10-13°C), which keeps growth compact and encourages winter flower buds. You can pick up a digital thermometer to take the guesswork out of it, such as the ThermoPro TP50 Digital Indoor Thermometer, available from Walmart, which can also flag up drafts you might not otherwise notice.

In November, the best thing you can do with your bottle of houseplant fertilizer is tuck it away in a cupboard until spring. Jade plants grow very little in the dark months: feeding them won't change that. They enter a natural dormancy phase during short, low-light winter days, and their roots can’t process the extra nutrients. Feeding a dormant succulent just forces out weak, pale shoots that stretch awkwardly toward the window and snap easily under their own weight.

Unused fertilizer salts can also accumulate rapidly in dry winter potting mix, burning delicate roots and leaving crusty mineral deposits. Whether you tend a classic green jade plant or a trailing Ripple Jade, hold off on all feeding until February. If you did feed in October, that's fine – just don't follow it up! Once bright spring sunlight sparks fresh leaf tips, you can resume feeding every 6-8 weeks through summer. At that point, use a balanced liquid succulent or houseplant fertilizer diluted to half strength.

Warm, dry indoor heating creates prime breeding conditions for sap-sucking houseplant pests, making a thorough inspection essential. Tip your pot gently toward bright window light and check the undersides of leaves and stem junctions. Look for tufts of white fuzz or sticky leaves: these are the telltale signs of citrus mealybugs (Planococcus citri). Any flat, brown, shell-like bumps are scale (Coccus hesperidum).

Industry observers note that quarantine affected plants. Dip a cotton swab in 70% isopropyl rubbing alcohol, such as Equate 70% Isopropyl Rubbing Alcohol from Walmart. Dab pests to dissolve their waxy protective coatings, repeating weekly until gone. Keep your jade plant in quarantine for a few weeks. Avoid insecticidal soaps on jade plants. Clemson University’s Home & Garden Information Center warns that fatty-acid soaps can damage jade foliage. While inspecting, pinch off any yellowing lower leaves. Dropping a few older bottom leaves after a fall move is normal. However, dark, mushy stems signal rot, requiring immediate action.

When a jade plant looks tired in November, resist the urge to try to fix everything at once. You might want to pull it out, give it a new pot and take the pruners to it, but you need to hold off on this. Roots that get disturbed now don't grow back rapidly, and big pruning cuts made now won't see new growth for months. Save routine repotting and shaping shears for spring, using a fast-draining cactus mix such as Espoma CA4 Organic Cactus Mix, available from Walmart, when the time comes.

Recent findings suggest that the only reason to repot now is if your plant has a rot emergency. If stems feel soft or the pot emits a sour odor, slide the plant out of its pot immediately. Trim away brown, rotted roots and soft stem tissue with sterilized snips. Let the calluses dry for a couple of days, then pot your jade into fresh, dry cactus mix. Hold off on water for a full week afterward. Don't let worry turn into extra watering. Too much water is one of the quickest ways to lose a jade in winter.

Caring for a jade plant in November is less about doing more, and more about stepping back thoughtfully. By scaling back your watering can, moving plants into bright southern light, guarding against chilly windows and drafts, shelving fertilizer, and keeping an eye out for winter pests, your jade will thrive. With a little attention now (and some cool, dark nights on your side), your jade may even reward you with pretty star-shaped winter blooms, before pushing out new leaves in spring.

Industry observers note that dogs are easy to love but, on occasion, are also surprisingly difficult to live with. Barking for no reason. The leash pulling that turns a simple walk into a tug-of-war. Turning the most expensive thing in the room into a chew toyâ¦.

In a recent development, most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits. But the truth is, there is often a reason behind these irritating habits. Dogs communicate through behavior, and what looks like a nuisance is sometimes a symptom of an unmet need. The trouble is that we often get distracted by tackling that symptom when we really need to dig deeper.

Understanding what is driving an annoying or unwanted behavior can make it much easier to address.

It has been revealed that dogs bark for many reasons, including boredom, anxiety, fear, a perceived threat, or a desire for attention. Any dog can develop a barking habit, regardless of size.

The key is identifying what triggers it. Boredom-related barking may improve with more exercise and mental stimulation, while anxiety or fear-based barking generally requires a more structured approach. Teaching a reliable "quiet" command and avoiding accidentally rewarding attention-seeking barking can also help.

Recent findings suggest that naturally vigilant dogs that spend their days standing guard at windows and alerting you to every passerby or suspicious-looking trash can may become less anxious if you block or obscure their view of the street. Limiting access to front-facing rooms or applying privacy film to windows can be a simple solution â if they canât see it, they stop worrying about it.

Chewing is normal for dogs, particularly teething puppies, but it becomes a problem when furniture, clothing, carpets, or walls become the preferred targets.

In a recent development, boredom and anxiety can contribute to destructive chewing, as can a lack of appropriate outlets. Keeping suitable chew toys available, putting valuable items out of reach, and managing the environment while the dog learns what is acceptable can help redirect the habit.

Sources indicate that A dog that greets visitors by launching itself at them has usually learned that jumping gets a response. Even pushing the dog away or telling it to stop can give them the attention theyâre seeking.

It has been revealed that ignoring the jumping and rewarding calm, four-paws-on-the-floor behavior teaches the dog that staying down gets the better response. Giving the dog an alternative behavior, such as sitting, can make the lesson clearer.

When faced with a friendly jumping dog, try the following:.

Keep your arms crossed, mouth closed, and eyes averted.

Turn your back, and walk away if they keep jumping.

Ignore them until they are calm and ready to listen to your command.

Recent findings suggest that dogs beg because it has worked before. Even one successful attempt at getting food from the table can establish the habit, making it particularly difficult to break.

Industry observers note that feeding the dog before your mealtimes can reduce the motivation to beg, while teaching it to settle in a designated spot gives it something else to do. The biggest challenge is consistency. Giving in occasionally can keep the behavior going.

Table scraps can also pose health risks because some common human foods are harmful to dogs, while regular extras can contribute to obesity.

Leash pulling can make an otherwise enjoyable walk exhausting. Dogs often pull because they are excited and have not learned that pulling does not make the walk happen faster.

According to recent reports, loose-leash training takes patience. Stopping whenever the leash becomes tight and continuing only when it becomes slack teaches the dog what behavior allows the walk to continue. Rewarding the dog for walking beside the handler can reinforce the lesson, while a well-fitted harness may provide additional control during training.

Different dogs need different equipment, and what works for a small dog is not necessarily going to be suitable for a large one. Talk to your vet about the safest and most effective option for you and your dog.

Poor recall is frustrating, but it can also be dangerous if your dog runs towards traffic or another dog.

Training should start in areas with few distractions before gradually becoming more challenging. High-value rewards can make coming back more appealing, while using the recall command for unpleasant situations can create a negative association that undermines the training.

Recent findings suggest that digging is instinctive for many dogs and can also be linked to boredom or excess energy. Trying to eliminate the behavior completely may not be the most practical approach; redirection has a much higher chance of success.

According to recent reports, create a designated digging area, such as a sandbox or corner of the yard, making sure there is a clear distinction between this and the rest of the garden. It may be unsightly, but laying down some temporary netting or a similar obstacle in the rest of the yard can help teach your dog where they can and cannot dig. Burying toys or treats there can make the spot more appealing, while increasing daily activity may reduce the urge to dig elsewhere.

Sources indicate that some dogs struggle when left alone. The resulting distress can include destructive behavior, excessive barking, and other difficult behaviors.

Gradually getting a dog used to being alone, starting with very short absences and slowly increasing them, is an evidence-based approach. Providing a comfortable, safe space can also help.

Recent findings suggest that avoid making a fuss of your dog when leaving the house or on your return â your comings and goings should become part of an ordinary day, not an event. More severe cases of separation anxiety may require veterinary input or help from a behaviorist.

Recent findings suggest that aggression can have many possible causes, including fear, poor socialization, pain, territorial behavior, or negative past experiences. Because the appropriate response depends on the cause, this is one behavior where professional help is particularly crucial.

A veterinary examination can help rule out an underlying medical problem, including pain. A qualified trainer or behaviorist can then help address the behavior using approaches such as positive reinforcement, desensitization, and counterconditioning. Punishment can make aggression worse rather than better.

Occasional accidents can happen, but frequent or sudden indoor elimination deserves attention.

According to recent reports, for dogs that are still learning, regular bathroom breaks and immediate positive reinforcement for going outside provide the foundation for housetraining. Enzymatic cleaners are useful for removing waste odors that can otherwise encourage a dog to return to the same spot.

If a previously house-trained dog suddenly begins having accidents, a check-up at the vet is appropriate to check for a possible medical cause.

Recent findings suggest that barking, chewing, jumping, digging, and the other behaviors on this list may be frustrating, but they rarely happen without a reason. Looking at what a dog is trying to communicate can reveal whether it needs more activity, clearer training, or a different kind of attention.

Addressing the underlying issue rather than simply trying to stop the behavior can make the problem easier to manage and help strengthen the relationship between you and your dog.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coneflowers (Echinacea spp.) are tough, low-maintenance perennials that are staples in many gardens.
  • Though considered low-care perennials, these flowers are about as close to no-care as a flower can be.
  • I’ve pulled together a list of the top five things to do – or not do – to your coneflowers in November while you're busy winterizing the garden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coneflowers (Echinacea spp.) are tough, low-maintenance perennials that are staples in many gardens. Their tall blooms bring long-lasting color and attract pollinators like bees and butterflies.

Though considered low-care perennials, these flowers are about as close to no-care as a flower can be. By the time November rolls around, these beautiful plants don’t need much. In fact, when you are growing coneflowers, it’s more key to know what to avoid than to complete a task list.

I’ve pulled together a list of the top five things to do – or not do – to your coneflowers in November while you're busy winterizing the garden. The primary goals are wildlife support, disease control, and frost protection.

Coneflowers bloom with cheerful, daisy-like flowers from early summer through fall. By November, the plants have faded, and cutting them back may seem like the obvious next step.

But don’t be tempted to prune coneflowers in the fall unless you are a total garden neatnik. It’s far better to wait to prune until spring. If you leave the dried seed heads standing, you give songbirds a valuable food source to help them make it through the winter. Goldfinches, chickadees, and cardinals will thank you. In addition, the hollow stems of the coneflowers provide habitat for overwintering beneficial insects. Plan to prune them in early spring.

Every rule has an exception, and it’s best not to prune coneflowers in November unless the foliage is diseased. Whenever you see sick foliage – in this case, coneflowers with powdery mildew, leaf spots, or aster yellows – it’s high time for a haircut.

According to recent reports, cut back any diseased or pest-infested coneflower stalks to a few inches above the soil. Toss all the trimmings in the trash, not the compost heap. Don’t forget to sanitize your pruners between plants and after you are done. Equate 91% Isopropyl Alcohol from Walmart is a handy option – simply dilute it to around 70% before using it to disinfect the blades.

If powdery mildew is a recurring problem, consider keeping Bonide Neem Oil Spray on hand for next growing season. Applied at the first signs of infection, it can help control the disease and prevent it from spreading, provided the product label covers the intended use.

Coneflowers are hardly prima donnas, but they do insist on well-draining soil. Waterlogged soil causes root and crown rot in coneflowers, sad endings for such beautiful perennials.

Recent findings suggest that the easiest way to check your flowers’ drainage is to wait for a late autumn rain. Let the rain do its thing, then – after an hour or two – head out to the coneflower bed and take a look. If you see standing water or water pooling on the soil for hours after the rain stops, your drainage is poor.

Recent findings suggest that poor drainage is not a death sentence. You can remedy this by layering a mixture of compost and, where appropriate, horticultural grit, such as this 1–2 mm coarse horticultural grit from Home Depot. This will redirect the flow of water away from the core roots.

You can consider transplanting the perennial in spring to a location with better drainage.

It has been revealed that organic mulch helps keep your coneflowers’ roots protected through the winter. Spread a loose layer – 2 to 3 inches (5–7.5 cm) deep – around the base of the plants to shield the root zone from extreme temperatures and keep weeds away.

Sources indicate that A natural shredded mulch, such as Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot, is a good choice. But take care: don’t let the mulch touch the main crown, or crown rot may develop.

Perennials with their roots in the ground are less vulnerable to winter temperatures than potted plants. While coneflowers are tall plants with stems that can reach 4 feet (1.2 m), dwarf varieties grow well in containers.

It has been revealed that these smaller perennials will come back every year if you provide them adequate winter protection. First, move the containers close to a structure in a sheltered spot. The Bamworld rolling plant caddies from Amazon make moving heavy pots much easier.

According to recent reports, if your hardiness zone is USDA 5–9, you may be able to overwinter them outside with adequate protection. Mound mulch around the pots for insulation, or try the leaf insulation trick. For extra protection, wrap the containers in a layer of Valibe frost-protection fabric.

In cooler zones, move your potted coneflowers into a cold, unheated garage or shed where their roots will be protected from extreme freezing temperatures. Keep the soil barely moist through dormancy, but never waterlogged, and empty any saucers after watering.

Think of these four tasks as the biggest things NOT to do with coneflowers in November. Avoiding them will almost guarantee your coneflowers greet spring happy and healthy.

According to recent reports, when my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

It has been revealed that itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

Any suggestions on what I could try?â.

You have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

Recent findings suggest that I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

Please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical concerns sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

That is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is at the moment looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

It has been revealed that rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

Industry observers note that the interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

It has been revealed that the Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

Sources indicate that lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

According to recent reports, living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

Industry observers note that the current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:.

Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation.

Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment.

Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

For families who decide to participate, it is notable to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

When it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

The recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

Sources indicate that there's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a substantial deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

Industry observers note that but this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

It has been revealed that aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesnât mean they canât contribute to canine aging research.

The Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

Itâs important to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

When it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

Recent findings suggest that and anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

Industry observers note that that's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

It has been revealed that for owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.

Sources indicate that my 1-year-old cat Daisy has allergies. She is on a special hydrolyzed diet. Iâm trying to find an allergen-neutralizing spray to cut back on dust mites in the house. Would you recommend any specific products?

Since Daisy is already on a hydrolyzed diet, it makes sense to look at environmental allergens too, especially if her allergic signs are continuing. Dust mites are common household allergens, and while the goal is to reduce the amount of allergens in her environment, eliminating them completely is not realistic. Regularly washing bedding and blankets, vacuuming with a HEPA filter, and keeping dust to a minimum are still the best places to start.

If you would like to try a spray, Purefy Anti-Allergen Spray works differently from an insecticide. It is intended to neutralize or remove the allergenic proteins associated with dust mite debris, particularly the proteins found in their feces and other microscopic particles that accumulate in household dust and fabrics. Those proteins, rather than the living mite itself, are an important source of the allergic reaction. So the idea is not to kill every mite in the house, but to reduce the allergen they leave behind.

I would specifically avoid routinely using insecticide or acaricide sprays around Daisy, even when a product is marketed as ânatural.â Cats can be particularly sensitive to certain botanical ingredients and insecticides, including some essential oils and pyrethroids. If you use an anti-allergen spray, follow the label carefully, keep Daisy away from treated surfaces until they are completely dry, ventilate the area well, and never spray it directly on her or on surfaces she is likely to lick. Please ensure you also keep it away from food and water bowls.

Recent findings suggest that think of the spray as an extra layer of environmental control, not a treatment for Daisy's allergy. The unglamorous combination of washing, HEPA vacuuming, and reducing dust is still doing most of the heavy lifting. And if Daisy continues to have significant allergic signs despite a properly conducted hydrolyzed diet trial and environmental management, it is worth investigating other possible triggers rather than simply reaching for stronger household chemicals. Usually, the answer is not a more powerful spray, but figuring out exactly what is making your cat itchy. So, real detective work is often needed for success.

Sources indicate that halloween packs a steady stream of costumed strangers and bowls of candy into a single evening, and for dogs that combination carries more hazards than most people expect. Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

Halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

Keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

Costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs important to pay attention to how they respond.

Industry observers note that A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

Recent findings suggest that A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

According to recent reports, there's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

Halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

In a recent development, A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

In a recent development, jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

Recent findings suggest that real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

In a recent development, the liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

Industry observers note that check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

According to recent reports, handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

In a recent development, closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

Industry observers note that keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly vital on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

Industry observers note that if a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

Check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

Halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

It's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

Legend has it that one of my earliest gardening forays involved a large lavender bush. As a toddler, I fell sideways into a mound of perfumed purple blooms and just lay there on my back, gazing at the bobbling petals, apparently with a look of absolute joy on my face. As a grown-up, the joy of lavender is still very much a thing. I may try to be more careful about where I stand these days, but my fascination with this sun-kissed fragrant icon is only getting more pronounced with time.

It has been revealed that few garden pleasures rival the velvety fix of fingers dancing along a billowing carpet of lavender wands on a languid summer afternoon. Beyond its timeless fragrance, lavender offers constant, lyrical movement and enduring cottage garden prettiness that seems to work in a range of palettes and plant combinations. Throw in a chorus of bumblebees drunk on nectar and swinging on those violet spires, and you can see why it’s so easy to fall head over heels for this Mediterranean beauty.

Sources indicate that bizarrely, lavender has a bit of a reputation for being tricky to grow, but the truth is that it’s the ultimate garden rebel. While many perennials long for luxuriant loam and scoops of compost, lavender is sculpted by lean, rocky soils and blistering sun, and it isn’t that hard to harness its intoxicating essential oils and maintain a tight, sturdy habit. Whether you want a petite purple knot garden or a sun-drenched lavender planter, this enduring favorite deserves a spot in every yard. Here’s how to ensure your plants return year after year with lush, aromatic blooms.

Recent findings suggest that lavandula spp. (L. angustifolia, L. stoechas, L. dentata, L. × intermedia).

1-3 feet (30-90cm) depending on species.
