The Right Types of Christmas Lights for Indoor and Outdoor Holiday Displays

📅 29 Sep 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Each year, as the holiday season approaches, homeowners prepare to deck their homes in sparkling lights.
  • More than 150 million strings of Christmas lights are sold in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Each year, as the holiday season approaches, homeowners prepare to deck their homes in sparkling lights. They pull tangled strings from their attics and garages and then, after rushing to the store for replacement bulbs, fuses, or even more lights, they get to work. But if they’re starting fresh in a new house or trying to change up their holiday decor, they have some lighting decisions to make: What kind of Christmas lights should they use? What are the best Christmas lights for the roof? Which lights should are best for the mantel?

More than 150 million strings of Christmas lights are sold in the U.S. every year. Homeowners certainly have a lot to choose from. This guide is the place to start. Here you’ll find some Christmas light basics, a review of the most common types of lights, and suggestions for the best uses for each type.

According to recent reports, first, decide whether you want LED or incandescent lights. The choice largely comes down to cost, energy efficiency, and aesthetics.

It has been revealed that since their introduction in the late 1990s, LED Christmas lights have become increasingly popular. In 2024, LED lights accounted for more than 90 percent of holiday string light sales, and for good reason. LED Christmas lights are far more energy efficient and last significantly longer than incandescent bulbs, going strong for upwards of 50,000 hours. Additionally, LED bulbs are brighter and stay cooler than incandescent bulbs. Also worth noting: While you can generally connect only three or so incandescent light strings together, you can link together many more LED strings, depending on their wattage. This can be a big help if you’re installing lights along an expansive roof or trimming an especially large tree.

LEDs do, however, have some significant negatives. For starters, they cost more than incandescents. However, because they last longer and are more energy efficient, the higher expense can be offset over time by lower utility costs and savings from not having to replace the lights as frequently. Another drawback: Some homeowners simply don’t like the look of LEDs, finding the light too harsh and their colors too cool. While newer LEDs have a greater range of color temperature and improved color rendering, some shoppers still prefer the cozier look of incandescents.

Best For: Those willing to pay a higher upfront cost in return for energy efficiency and a vibrant display.

Our Recommendation: Connectable 240 LED Twinkle Fairy Light String at Amazon for $17.99These LED wide-angle indoor/outdoor lights extend to a length of 88 feet, offer 13 lighting modes, and are available in a range of colors.

It has been revealed that incandescent lights are typically less expensive than LEDs and emit a warmer, softer glow. However, incandescent bulbs burn out faster, are less durable, and consume a lot more electricity than LED bulbs.

Best For: Creating a nostalgic display with a warmer, cozier glow.

Our Recommendation: Home Accents Holiday 300 Incandescent Mini String Lights at The Home Depot for $9.98Even if one of the bulbs burns out, this 68-foot strand of 300 mini incandescent lights will stay lit; available in white and multicolor.

Holiday lights are rated for outdoor use, indoor use only, or indoor/outdoor use.

Industry observers note that in a 2026 survey by Thumbtack, over half of respondents proposal to hang holiday lights outdoors this year. If you’re part of this majority, be sure that you’re using outdoor-rated holiday lights for your outdoor Christmas light installations. These lights are more weather-resistant, have thicker wiring, and are made of more durable materials than indoor Christmas lights. Other tips for selecting and hanging outdoor lights include:.

According to recent reports, the Balsam Hill classic spruce tree is well-made, easy to set up, and sturdy enough to hang heavy ornaments. See our full review.

It has been revealed that christmas lights can be powered by electricity, batteries, solar energy, or even USB. Your budget and access to electrical outlets will help you determine which power sources are best for your situation.

Plug-in lights are any type of light that plugs into an electrical socket. This is the traditional way of powering Christmas lights.

For plug-in lights, you need a nearby electrical outlet or an extension cord. Once plugged in, the lights stay on as long as there’s power. There’s no need to worry about dead batteries or the solar charge depleting.

Best For: Creating dependable, long-lasting holiday light displays near a power outlet or where an extension cord can be used.

Our Recommendation: Prextex 100-Count White Christmas Lights at Amazon for $8.99This 20-foot incandescent light string has 100 warm white lights with a waterproof design suitable for indoor or outdoor use.

Sources indicate that some holiday lights rely on battery power, often using AA batteries. These sets are great solutions in situations where cords could pose a tripping hazard. where you want to keep the power source hidden, or where there are no electrical outlets nearby—for instance, if you want to add lights to a Christmas wreath on an entry door.

Recent findings suggest that the lifespan of battery-operated lights can vary depending on the number of lights on the strand, whether the bulbs are LED or incandescent, the quality of the batteries, and other factors. While some lights may stay lit for more than 100 hours before requiring latest batteries, others will need fresh batteries after only a few hours.

Best For: Displaying lights where no power outlets are available or where cords either aren’t wanted or can’t be used.

Sources indicate that our Recommendation: Loende Battery-Operated String Lights at Amazon for $12.99These classic-looking LED string lights are available in white, clear, and multicolor. The 50-light, 18-foot string features eight lighting modes and an automatic timer.

Solar-powered Christmas lights offer an eco-friendly solution for holiday decorations. Rather than consuming electricity, these lights are powered by sunlight through a connected solar panel. Solar Christmas lights are often comparably priced to their plug-in LED counterparts.

Recent findings suggest that though they’re eco-friendly, be forewarned that the lights may not stay lit very long at night if the solar panel doesn’t receive enough sunlight during the day. Also, if you’re planning a large display, the individual solar panels of each light strand could leave your lawn looking cluttered.

Best For: Small outdoor areas that get a lot of sunlight, such as sunny pathways, small sections of fence, and shrubs.

It has been revealed that our Recommendation: Joomer Solar Christmas Lights 2 Pack at Amazon for $19.99 Available in white and multicolor as well as several single-color options, this two-pack totals 400 LED lights and 144 feet and is safe for indoor and outdoor use. The strands offer eight lighting modes, and a 6-hour charge during the day will power the lights for more than 8 hours.

According to recent reports, plug these lights into a laptop, power bank, USB power adapter, or anywhere else you find a USB port. They’re handy for brightening up bedrooms, backyards, campsites, and other spots where a USB port is the most convenient power option.

Best For: Any space where a USB port is the most easily accessible power source for spreading some holiday cheer.

Our Recommendation: Green Convenience 100 LED USB or Battery String Lights at Amazon for $9.99This 33-foot indoor/outdoor holiday light string can be powered with either batteries or USB, offers eight lighting modes, comes with a remote control and timer function, and is available in white or multicolor.

Once you’ve decided whether you want LED or incandescent lights and have figured out how you’ll power them, it’s time to choose the best Christmas lights to suit your holiday decor. Here’s a rundown of the most common string and bulb styles and some of their best uses.

These small cylindrical bulbs with pointy tips are the most common holiday string lights. They’re available with both LED and incandescent bulbs and are sold for both indoor and outdoor use. Though they’re probably the most popular types of Christmas tree lights, mini string lights are also great for highlighting the mantel, wrapping around columns and banisters, and draping over entryways and windows. These are the light strings you’ll find crowding the shelves at the best places to find Christmas lights.

Recent findings suggest that there are two main types of mini lights: M5 bulbs and T5 bulbs. Their shapes are similar, but T5 bulbs have a pointier tip, while M5 bulbs have a more rounded tip and textured sides.

Best For: Decorating Christmas trees and hanging over windows and entryways.

Our Recommendation: Minetom LED Christmas Mini Lights, Warm White at Amazon for $16.99Give a warm glow to your Christmas tree, bushes, columns, and more with this 75-foot string of 200 indoor/outdoor mini lights that offers eight lighting modes.

For a vintage look, nothing beats classic, colorful C6, C7, and C9 bulbs. Their rounded, conical shape evokes the homey Christmas trees in movies like It’s a Wonderful Life and A Christmas Story.

These days, C-type bulbs are available in both incandescent and LED light strings and in a range of colors. Use the smaller C6 (1⅛ inches tall) or C7 bulbs (1½ inches tall) indoors to give the Christmas tree or mantel a retro vibe, or outside on smaller trees and architectural features. The larger C9 bulbs (2½ inches tall) are best used outside to frame the roof or windows, or to wrap larger trees and shrubs.

C6 and C7, Best For: Lighting retro-style Christmas trees and smaller landscaping features.

Our Recommendation: Dazzle Bright C6 Christmas String Lights at Amazon for $16.99This set of indoor/outdoor C6 Christmas lights has 100 multicolor LED bulbs and eight lighting modes; UL-certified, and can be used indoors or outdoors.

Our Recommendation: Minetom C7 Christmas String Lights at Amazon for $33.99This 50-foot string has 52 C7 bulbs that are transparent, warm white, and give a vintage glow.

C9, Best For: Illuminating a large roofline.

Our Recommendation: Wintergreen 25 C9 Multicolor LED Christmas Lights at Amazon for $22.99This 17-foot string of faceted, indoor/outdoor C9 LED bulbs is expandable (you can safely connect up to 90 sets), long-lasting, and even dimmable.

Also known as 5mm lights, these bulbs have a concave lens that spreads extremely bright light in all directions. Because they’re compact, they don’t snag as easily as larger lights, so they’re often the bulb of choice for wrapping tree trunks and branches. Don’t let their small size fool you—these lights can easily illuminate large spaces.

Best For: Wrapping branches, bushes, or trees.

Our Recommendation: Wintergreen Lighting Multicolor 5mm LED Christmas Lights at Amazon for $24.99Available in white, single-color, and a variety of color combinations, this 24-foot strand of 70 LEDs is backed by a 3-year seasonal warranty—and you can string together 44 sets.

Sources indicate that strings of icicle lights have short, vertical strands of mini lights (or actual icicle-shaped bulbs) hanging down at intervals, “dripping” like icicles. They’re available in both LED and incandescent, and although white icicle lights are most popular, they’re also available in multicolor and single-color strands.

Best For: Installing on eaves to mimic dripping icicles.

Industry observers note that our Recommendation: Knonew Christmas Icicle Lights at Amazon for $69.99This 99-foot string of icicle lights features 228 vertical drops, eight modes, and a built-in timer. Also available in multicolor and single-color strands.

Industry observers note that pathway lights are mounted on stakes that can be driven into the ground along walkways, driveways, or garden beds to enhance safety and spread holiday joy. These eye-catching outdoor decorations are typically plug-in or solar-powered and available in fanciful shapes like candy canes, jolly Santas, and Christmas bulbs.

Best For: Lining front walkways or driveways.

In a recent development, our Recommendation: Brightown C9 Christmas String Lights LED Pathway Lights at Amazon for $32.99With 20 C9 bulbs on a 25.7-foot string, these plug-in LED pathway lights will brighten up walkways and garden beds. They’re also available in faceted and multicolor styles.

Sources indicate that add a bright, modern, geometric touch to your outdoor decor with durable, flexible rope lights. They’re easy to bend around railings and columns, and some strands offer color-changing or chasing effects.

Best For: Wrapping tree trunks and banisters, and accenting architectural features.

Our Recommendation: Wintergreen Lighting 18-Foot LED Warm White Rope Lights at Amazon for $27.99The kit includes an 18-foot length of rope with 216 LED bulbs, mounting clips, three splice connectors, and end caps. Connect up to 15 kits; available in multicolor and various color combinations as well as single-color options.

Recent findings suggest that net lights are light strings that have been connected into a grid. They’re a hassle-free way to create a uniform blanket of light on bushes and hedges. Similarly, trunk lights are nets designed to wrap around the trunk of a tree. Both products can really speed up holiday decorating.

To make sure you’re buying the right size, first measure the square footage (surface area) of the shrub you’d like to cover. Net lights generally range from 4 to 10 feet long and 2 to 5 feet wide, although they can run much larger.

Best For: Covering shrubs and hedges with lights.

Our Recommendation: Meteds 120 LED Christmas Net Lights at Amazon for $23.39The warm white bulbs in this 6-by-4-foot net light will give your shrub a romantic glow, but it’s also available in cool white as well as three colorful options. Connect up to 10 sets.

Many of the LED light options in this list are available with color-changing features, where bulbs produce many different hues, or “chasing” features, where bulbs cycle on and off in patterns that create the illusion of lights moving along the string. These technological wonders may be the most fun and interactive types of Christmas tree lighting, and whether they’re used indoors or out, they give the homeowner the ability to customize or reimagine their holiday decorating scheme at a moment’s notice, often using a remote or an app.

Best For: Creating dynamic, customizable holiday light displays, indoors and outside.

Our Recommendation: Twinkly Strings Smart LED Christmas Lights at Amazon for $74.99Once you’ve mapped your light display to the company’s app, you can select one of the app’s preset light effects or create your own, with 16 million colors to choose from.

The colors you choose set the tone for your holiday light display: the classy, subdued sparkle of a warm white, the exuberance of a multicolor string, or the uniform glow of a single hue. Consider some of these popular choices.

For the Christmas tree: Strategy on at least 100 lights per vertical foot of tree, more if the tree is especially wide or if you like a really bright tree.

For shrubs: Net lights are the fastest and easiest way to illuminate bushes. Just measure the approximate surface area of the bush and purchase a net light that will cover it. If you’re using string lights, figure 50 lights per square foot.

For the exterior: Decide where you want to install lights. Do you want them just along the eaves, or would you like to outline windows, railings, and other architectural features? Measure the total linear feet you intend to cover, add 10 percent to account for corners, plug-in space, and irregularities, and then divide by the length of your light strands (for example, 25 feet or 50 feet) to determine how many you’ll need.

For wrapping columns/tree trunks: The number of lights needed will vary depending on the circumference and height of the column, the desired vertical spacing of the lights, and the distance between lights on the string (for mini lights, the standard is 4 or 6 inches). To make things easier, check online for calculators.

How to Get Stink Bugs Out of Your House

📅 18 Nov 2015 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • The brown marmorated stink bug (Halyomorpha halys) is a stowaway from Asia that entered the U.S.
  • Industry observers note that as of 2021, the brown marmorated stink bug had been found in 47 states, and it’s earned a rep as an agricultural villain, feeding on upward of 60 different species of fruits, vegetables, and ornamental plants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

The brown marmorated stink bug (Halyomorpha halys) is a stowaway from Asia that entered the U.S. sometime in the 1990s. Adult stink bugs are approximately the size of a dime and easily recognized by their shield shape, mottled gray-brown coloring, and alternating light and dark bands on their antennae and abdomen. They can also, of course, be identified by the unpleasant odor they release, often described as a strong cilantro-like smell, when they are threatened or squashed. (Not everyone is sensitive to the smell, so it’s possible to have an infestation even if you don’t perceive the odor.).

Industry observers note that as of 2021, the brown marmorated stink bug had been found in 47 states, and it’s earned a rep as an agricultural villain, feeding on upward of 60 different species of fruits, vegetables, and ornamental plants. But its habits have also made it a notable household nuisance.

Outdoors, stink bugs are attracted to a wide range of plants. But when the weather turns cold and they start searching for a place to spend the winter, they, like so many other bugs, seek the warmth and shelter of your home. In these colder months, they enter a dormant phase during which they’re inactive, neither feeding nor reproducing. In fact, they’re model insect houseguests: They don’t move around much, damage structures or clothing, reproduce, or bite people or animals. Stink bugs are not poisonous, and they won’t raid the pantry.

According to recent reports, stink bugs do, however, have some significant drawbacks, including their noxious odor. Unfortunately, they also release a pheromone that attracts other stink bugs, which means they can gather in numbers reaching into the hundreds or even thousands.

In a recent development, while dormant, stink bugs may move around slowly, if at all. You are most likely to notice them in the fall, when they’re coming indoors, or in early spring as they head back outside to mate. David Price, associate certified entomologist and director of technical services at Mosquito Joe, a Neighborly company, “They do not leave behind any visible indications they have chosen your home, other than their physical appearance.” This means that you might not know you have a stink bug infestation until you actually see a bug, dead or alive.

In a recent development, commercial insecticides may kill off some of the stink bugs in your house, but these toxic chemicals are generally ineffective and don’t offer a long-term solution. “Their shield provides them with protection against many insecticides,” Price says. Even after treatment, bugs can migrate from other areas of the house or emerge from cracks and crevices, including gaps around baseboards and molding. Insecticides do nothing to prevent more bugs from coming in, either. If you’re trying to figure out how to eliminate stink bugs, the most effective approaches are physical removal and deterrence.

According to recent reports, for physical removal, focus on areas where stink bugs tend to congregate. Price notes that they typically gather in the “attic, or voids around windows,” and they’re attracted to light-colored surfaces and the sunny side of a house. Stink bugs are also known to tuck themselves into folds of curtains, hole up in crevices, and seek out quiet spots like crawl spaces.

Industry observers note that you can use either a regular vacuum or a wet/dry vacuum, but use just the hose. Steer clear of attachments that might crush the bugs. You will need to clean out the vacuum when done. While the smell will eventually wear off, if your home is subject to frequent infestations, you may want to invest in a dedicated vacuum or handheld vac. Another option: Slip a knee-high stocking over the vacuum hose, secure it with a rubber band, and stuff the toe of the stocking down the hose so the stink bugs will be captured in the stocking instead of the vacuum canister.

Industry observers note that if you are sweeping up stink bugs with a broom, it’s a good idea to sweep or dump them directly into a bucket of soapy water. Dispose of the bugs outside the house in a tied plastic bag.

Sources indicate that A direct hit with a stream of soapy water from a spray bottle should kill a stink bug. It takes just a few teaspoons of dish soap in a spray bottle filled with water.

Trapping stink bugs when they’re on the move is an inexpensive but effective strategy, especially in the spring, when the brighter, longer days signal that it’s time for them to head outside and mate.

The Flowtron bug zapper has an electrified grid that is effective at killing insects, though its design may not be for everyone. Read the review.

According to recent reports, A spritz of hair spray can paralyze a stink bug so you can either drop it in a bucket of soapy water or simply take it outside. Take care using this method near upholstery, leather, and other surfaces that could be damaged by hair spray.

Sources indicate that stink bugs are attracted to light, including the blue UV light that bug zappers use. While not the most effective method, a quality bug zapper can be a useful ally. Note that entomologists and others concerned with the environment discourage the use of zappers, which kill both good and bad bugs.

It has been revealed that if you’ve successfully eliminated stink bugs from your home, you’ll continue to have problems if you can’t prevent more bugs from coming in. The key to keeping stink bugs out is to seal common entry points.

Fill cracks around windows and doors, both indoors and out, with exterior caulk.

Check around plumbing pipes, AC lines, cables, electrical conduits, and other pipes that pass through the exterior walls of your home. Seal up gaps, indoors and out, with plumber’s putty, sealant, spray foam, or another appropriate filler.

It has been revealed that periodically, and certainly before fall kicks in, check your home’s siding for gaps and holes. Caulk gaps as needed.

Sources indicate that make sure there are no openings to the outside (check for daylight showing through). Also, look for cracks in the walls.

When possible, remove window air conditioners at summer’s end. If they must stay in all year, seal up any gaps around the unit and cover it before the weather turns colder.

Check weatherstripping around doors for wear and tear, such as missing pieces and other damage. Replace weatherstripping as necessary.

In a recent development, look for rips and tears in window or door screens, and repair or replace damaged screens promptly. Invest in screens if some of your windows or doors don’t have them.

Screen gable vents, eave vents, and other openings to prevent stink bugs from gaining access.

In a recent development, all of the sealing methods rank high in advice for how to deter stink bugs from invading your house. A bonus method is use of various essential oils, especially clove, lemongrass, spearmint, and ylang-ylang, which can discourage stink bugs from coming in. Combine about 10 or so drops of the essential oil of your choice (or a combination of a few oils) with water in a spray bottle, and spray windowsills, window frames, doorways, and other common entry points regularly in fall. Another option is to mix a few teaspoons of garlic powder with a few cups of water and spray the solution around entry points.

It has been revealed that these removal and deterrence strategies can help control a modest infestation, but if you’ve tried all of these and your home is still overwhelmed by hundreds of stink bugs, you need a pro. Pest control companies can employ multiple techniques to stop an infestation, including vacuuming, applying specialized dusts and powders, and sealing off or treating entry points. They also can provide advice on preventing future infestations.

Keeping a home properly sealed prevents stink bugs from entering. It’s notable to check the perimeter and openings annually, and seal or weatherstrip as needed.

Rake up debris and edible vegetation around your home’s foundation, keep wood piles and compost heaps well away from the house, and consider turning off interior and exterior lights near entrances when possible.

Although this is a common belief, killing a stink bug does not attract others.

Recent findings suggest that yes, you can flush stink bugs down the toilet. Flushing is a good way to get rid of them without giving them a chance to release their scent.

Vacuuming is the fastest and most efficient way to remove stink bugs. For easy disposal, use a vacuum with a bag.

Industry News: How To Spot a Flood-Damaged Car Before You Buy It

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Learn the subtle signs to look for to avoid buying a flooded car.
  • With the average cost of a fresh car approaching $50,000, it can make more financial sense to buy used.
  • According to recent reports, use your nose to detect water damage inside the vehicle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Learn the subtle signs to look for to avoid buying a flooded car.

With the average cost of a fresh car approaching $50,000, it can make more financial sense to buy used. But, while the lower price point is appealing, mechanic David Martin indicates to shop carefully and to check any used car for signs of flooding. “Engine computers, sensors, electrical connectors and wiring are vulnerable to corrosion, expensive to fix and could endanger lives,” he says. Not all cars that have been in a flood will be given a flood title, and unscrupulous sellers will mask this fact from would-be buyers. Ahead, learn how to tell if you’re buying a flood-damaged car, with expert-backed advice from Martin.

According to recent reports, use your nose to detect water damage inside the vehicle. “If the car smells musty or moldy, watch out,” Martin states. “Also, pay attention to cars that have strong air freshener or detergent scents. They could be used to mask flood-related mildew.” Additionally, look for silt or mud in glove compartments or under seats where it may have been overlooked during cleaning. Finding it is a tell-tale sign the car has been flooded. Also look carefully for condensation behind instrument panels and interior and exterior lights.

Recent findings suggest that check for any rust or flaking metal on the car’s underside, especially on brake lines and around the fuel tank, Martin says. Lift the hood and look for corrosion on the battery terminals and engine components, then open the car doors and inspect the door hinges for signs of rust.

In a recent development, vehicle upholstery and carpeting can reveal signs of flooding. Feel for dampness and look for stains, as well as loose, wrinkled or buckled carpeting. Additionally, pull seat belts all the way out to check for stains, mildew or mud and look for mismatched or recently replaced carpeting and upholstery.

Turn on the car and do a thorough test of the car’s electrical components. Check the power windows, door locks, seat controls, and backup camera. “Make sure all lights, the air conditioner, heater, wipers, turn signals, stereo and navigation systems work,” Martin indicates. “And test them more than once.” Even if an electrical component is working, check to make sure it’s working properly. Flickering lights and intermittent functioning can also be signs of water damage.

Recent findings suggest that flood-damaged cars may be moved across state lines and retitled, so always get a Carfax report, which tracks a vehicle’s complete history regardless of location. Additionally, run the vehicle’s VIN number through the National Insurance Crime Bureau. “The service can identify whether a car has been reported stolen or labeled as salvage by insurance companies due to flooding,” Martin says. “But, while these reports can be helpful, they don’t cover everything.That’s why having a certified mechanic inspect a used car before you buy is a smart investment.”.

In a recent development, even if you don’t suspect a car has been flooded after looking it over yourself, a professional mechanic could catch subtle signs you missed, as well as any other mechanical challenges with the vehicle. Ask them to specifically check for signs of flooding.

Yes, a flood-damaged car can still have a clean title and show no record of flooding in its history.

No, not if you intend to drive it. Issues can continue to arise years after a flooding event that can impact the vehicle’s functioning. However, you could buy a flooded car with the intention of using it for parts.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve tested our fair share of kitchen appliances over the years, and for our money, a good water filter is one of the most practical investments you can make. From removing tap water’s harsh taste and smell to catching invisible and unhealthy contaminants, countertop reverse osmosis systems make access to crisp, clean drinking water easy.

Sources indicate that in our recent head-to-head testing of the best countertop water filters, the Bluevua Ropot countertop reverse osmosis water filter system earned the top spot. It wasn’t just the five-stage filtration that won us over—it was the combination of NSF- and WQA-certification, the no-installation setup, and the fact that the filters last up to 2 years, all wrapped in a design that won’t look out of place next to your coffee maker.

It has been revealed that performance is perhaps the most important aspect of a water filter, and the Ropot’s is excellent: water passes through a sediment filter, a pre-carbon block, a high-precision reverse osmosis (RO) membrane, a post-carbon filter, and a remineralization stage. Unlike some competitors, Bluevua backs this unit’s performance with actual NSF and WQA certification.

The downside of such thorough filtration is that the process takes longer than it would with a basic pitcher filter, meaning the Ropot isn’t for you if you’re not going to be diligent about refilling it in advance. But if you can get into the habit of refilling the reservoir after every couple of glasses, it’ll be well worth it. Not only will the five-stage filtration process remove contaminants (including sediment, chlorine, heavy metals, fluoride, PFAS, microplastics, pesticides, dissolved solids, and bad tastes and odors), but it goes the extra mile with a remineralization stage that adds beneficial minerals back in, like calcium and magnesium. In our taste tests against tap water, pitcher filters, and other RO systems, the Ropot’s flavor was easily one of the best.

Recent findings suggest that while reverse osmosis systems are hard to beat in terms of filtration performance, they’re traditionally a bit rough when it comes to installation. But since the Bluevua Ropot is a countertop unit, there’s zero drilling or plumbing necessary. You just set it on the counter, plug it in, and fill the removable 1.77-liter tank. The digital panel highlights live total dissolved solids (TDS) readings alongside filter-life indicators, so you know when it’s time to change them out. When that time comes, the cartridges twist out and in without tools.

In a recent development, we also loved the high-borosilicate glass pitcher. Some of the others we tested didn’t come with a collection chamber for the filtered water at all, and if they did, they were often plastic (which can absorb odors or degrade over time). Bluevua’s glass carafe keeps purified water fresh and fits neatly in the refrigerator if cold water is what you prefer.

In terms of downsides, the Ropot was one of the more expensive water filters we tested, and the slower flow rate and larger footprint are real considerations if speed or space are your priorities. But between the certified filtration, the 2-year filter life, and water that consistently tasted better than bottled, we think it’s worth it.

Flat top griddles are great for cooking all kinds of foods, including those you’d never throw on a standard grill, which is why they’re such great sidekicks for tailgating and camping trips. These smaller flat-top griddles are also ideal for those who want one but don’t have enough deck or patio space for a full-sized outdoor griddle.

According to recent reports, I recently tested a newly introduced entrant in the portable griddle market: Weber’s 22-inch Slate griddle. While the Slate offers the rock-solid build quality and refined temperature controls we at Bob Vila have come to expect from Weber, it comes at a price, both in terms of cost and weight. The Slate is one of the most expensive and heaviest portable griddles we’ve tested. I’ve spent several months using the Weber Slate 22-inch griddle to cook a variety of foods and found it worth the weight and price thanks to impressive cooking performance and rock-solid build quality.

In a recent development, the Weber Slate 22-inch griddle is one of the largest portable tabletop griddles I’ve seen. With its 352 square inches of cooking surface, you can fit a lot of food on the griddle at once. And since it has two burners, you can create two large cooking zones. This came in handy when cooking meals that require two different temperatures, such as beef and peppers for fajitas or bacon and pancakes for breakfast.

It has been revealed that while size and weight obviously matter a great deal when it comes to portable griddles, performance is also crucial. The Weber Slate heats the carbon steel cooking surface with two burners totaling 16,000 BTUs. That isn’t particularly impressive—for comparison, Blackstone’s 22-inch tabletop griddle puts out a whopping 24,000 BTUs—but Weber makes up for it with its smart design. The Slate’s burners sit very close to the cooking surface, so more heat is directly transferred to the carbon steel plate. It also has built-in wind guards that prevent heat loss, so the heat generated by the burners can build up under the cooking surface. And once the griddle gets going, the carbon steel plate retains heat exceptionally well.

During testing, it took about 10 minutes to reach 500 degrees Fahrenheit with the lid closed. While this isn’t as hot as other portable tabletop griddles I’ve tested, the Weber also offered great low-temperature control. I was able to keep it at under 300 degrees Fahrenheit, which is among the lowest consistent temperatures I’ve been able to maintain on any griddle. How did that translate while cooking? The Weber packed enough heat to sear restaurant-worthy smashburgers but still offered enough low-temperature control to fry eggs and cook pancakes without burning them.

We’ve come to expect top-notch materials and build quality with Weber’s grills, and the Weber Slate 22-inch griddle didn’t disappoint. Anyone who’s used a griddle knows how hard it is to keep the surface from accruing rust, even when stored in a dry shed or garage. Weber case-hardens the Slate’s cooktop, which makes its cooking surface rust-resistant. Most griddles I’ve tested developed rust on the cooking surface even when cleaned, oiled, and sitting in my garage. The Weber remained rust-free, even when I neglected to clean it after cooking for several weeks.

In a recent development, that said, there are a few trade-offs for that expansive cooking surface, multi-burner design, and solid build quality. One is its weight. At 53.5 pounds, it’s far heavier than other top tabletop flat top griddles. In fact, it’s about 20 pounds heavier than the Blackstone 22, which has a similar cooking surface, and more than twice as heavy as the Pit Boss two-burner griddle. While I was able to carry the griddle over short distances without help, I found myself having to lighten the load by removing the cooktop, which meant I had to make two trips when moving it.

In a recent development, the Weber Slate also comes with a steeper price tag. At $379, it’s far more expensive than other similarly sized portable griddles, including the Cuisinart 22-inch tabletop griddle ($290) and the Blackstone 22-inch tabletop griddle ($219). The price difference is significant, but its build quality, rust-resistant top, and exceptional performance make it worth the additional cost.

#44176. What the Heck Happened To Regular Gear Shifts?

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1616 w)

What the Heck Happened To Regular Gear Shifts?

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that why ate regular gear shifts being replaced by increasingly impractical buttons and screens?
  • You sit down in the driver’s seat of your car, push the start button, and then reach for the gear lever.
  • In a recent development, there was a time when shifting gears was one of the most fundamental parts of driving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Sources indicate that why ate regular gear shifts being replaced by increasingly impractical buttons and screens? Here's the deal.

You sit down in the driver’s seat of your car, push the start button, and then reach for the gear lever. Except it’s not there. The console has ten cup holders and three phone charging ports, but no gear shift. Nothing above it on the dash either: that’s also lever-lackin’. Upon the column like an old school pickup? Nope.

In a recent development, there was a time when shifting gears was one of the most fundamental parts of driving. You reached for a lever, moved it into position, and felt a mechanical connection between your hand and the machinery responsible for making the car move. Whether you drove a three-on-the-tree sedan, a four-speed muscle car, or a truck with a modern automatic, there was a lever involved in changing gears.

Then automakers decided that shifting gears was probably too much work.

Today’s vehicles increasingly replace conventional gear selectors with things that are decidedly not gear selectors. Rotary knobs, push buttons, electronic switches, touchscreen menus, and all manner of non-levers are now in vogue.

The question is simple: What happened to gear shifts, and why did automakers decide that one of the most recognizable controls in an automobile needed reinventing?

Sources indicate that early automobiles required direct mechanical connections between the driver’s controls and the transmission. Whether automatic or manual, gearboxes used levers and linkages to move internal components into position to make the vehicle drive. The gear lever was a functional necessity.

As automatic transmissions became more common in the 1960s, the familiar PRND (Park, Reverse, Neutral, Drive) arrangement became standard. Whether mounted on the steering column or the center console, the selector offered a straightforward interface with an obvious purpose. And it was usually physically connected to what it was doing in the transmission.

It has been revealed that the mechanical connection also provided useful feedback. Moving a lever into Drive felt different from selecting Reverse or Park. The driver could often determine the selected gear by feel without looking down at the shifter.

It has been revealed that msst recently, however, electronic controls began replacing mechanical linkages. Known as shift-by-wire, these systems communicate the driver’s selection electronically rather than relying on a direct physical connection between the selector and transmission. By the 2010s this was the norm in consumer vehicles and the disconnection between driver and machine began in earnest.

This technology offered automakers more freedom in where and how they placed gear controls. It also opened the door to an increasingly strange assortment of alternatives. With the advent of increasingly smartphone-on-wheels designs, making the gear shift a radical part of design is now all the rage.

According to recent reports, once a conventional mechanical linkage was no longer necessary, designers gained considerable freedom. A rotary dial could perform the same function as a traditional lever. A collection of buttons could accomplish the same task. A small electronic toggle could select Drive or Reverse without occupying much space.

Some manufacturers embraced the change enthusiastically.

Sources indicate that jaguar Land Rover became particularly associated with rotary gear selectors, including the rising dial used in certain Jaguar and Land Rover models. Chrysler experimented with rotary selectors in vehicles such as the Ram 1500 (swiftly finding out that many truck owners hate them), while Ford and other manufacturers introduced electronic switches and compact selectors across portions of their lineups. Honda famously went to push buttons that were immediately compared to the (questionable, short-lived) push-button shifting American Motors used in the 1950s.

Sources indicate that mercedes-Benz moved many gear selectors to a steering-column stalk, freeing space on the center console. Not wanting to be left behind, Hyundai did the same, but with bulkier shifters located down low on the column. Others kept a traditional-appearing shifter, but made it barely move and difficult to shift into neutral (Nissan) or manual control (Subaru).

The reasoning isn’t entirely unreasonable. A conventional shifter can consume valuable cabin space, particularly in vehicles with complex center consoles. Replacing it with a dial or switch can free room for storage, cupholders, charging pads, and other amenities.

Electronic selectors can also reduce the number of mechanical components required between the cabin and transmission.

But there is a difference between making a control smaller and making it better.

According to recent reports, A conventional lever communicates something to the driver through its position and movement. A rotary dial or momentary switch often depends on a display or indicator to communicate the selected gear. The control becomes less self-explanatory, and the driver may need to look down to confirm what the vehicle is doing.

That isn’t necessarily a deal-breaker, but it raises an obvious question: What problem was the new design solving for the person behind the wheel? This question often goes unanswered.

Automotive interiors have become battlegrounds for designers seeking to make each latest model feel more modern than the last. Large screens, minimalist dashboards, floating center consoles, and increasingly elaborate ambient lighting have become selling points. Traditional physical controls can appear old-fashioned in comparison.

In a recent development, and despite design trends toward “minimalism” in vehicle cabins, prospective buyers are expecting more. We want cup holders capable of increasingly large volumes. We want phone chargers so we don’t have to plug anything in. We want a place to put a purse. An extra drink. Our miscellaneous devices. Car keys. A picture of grandma.

Despite design trends pushing toward minimalism, American car buyers are anything but minimal with the amount of stuff we expect to fit in our cars. A current, full-sized pickup truck will have no fewer than six drink holders within the driver’s reach. Because that’s what focus groups demand. Holes in the center console for a purse? Yep, also demanded in most SUVs and minivans. Two or more wireless phone chargers? Also requested. Set-and-forget climate controls? Thumbs up there too. Plugs for dash cams, a place for the air freshener that isn’t the rearview, a way to get into the center storage bin from at least four of the vehicle’s seating positions, six ways to put… You get the idea. We want a lot. While being minimal. Because that aesthetic is in.

So the conventional gear lever became an option that could be eliminated to make more space for other stuff, while achieving a minimalist look. And so the gear shift… Well, shifted to somewhere else.

Some of the alternatives make no sense whatsoever.

The problem isn’t that electronic shifters are inherently bad. It’s that automakers sometimes appear to treat novelty as an improvement in itself. A control that performs the same task in a less intuitive way hasn’t necessarily advanced automotive technology. It may simply have changed the shape of the inconvenience.

Much of the more recent change has come thanks to electric vehicles accelerating the transformation.

According to recent reports, most battery-electric vehicles don’t use conventional multi-gear transmissions. Their electric motors can deliver useful torque across a broad operating range, allowing many EVs to operate with a single fixed reduction gear rather than the multiple forward ratios common in gasoline-powered vehicles.

Drivers still need to select Park, Reverse, Neutral, and Drive, but there is less reason to retain a traditional transmission selector designed around a conventional automatic gearbox.

Industry observers note that add in that many EVs have been just experimental smartphones with wheels, and things get even dicier. Early adopters of a newly introduced technology are usually happy to accept all kinds of radical changes and inconveniences for the privilege of being first. And so gear shifters got radicalized in electric cars.

Some EVs use steering-column stalks. Others employ center-console switches, small toggles, or touchscreen controls. The absence of a conventional transmission also gives designers more freedom when arranging the cabin. Things could be sleeker, thinner, lower, and above all.. Whiter. Every early EV seemed to have a white interior with a complete absence of useful buttons or switches. Giant TV-sized screens dominated the interior instead.

However, electrification doesn’t automatically justify every unusual design. An EV still needs a clear, accessible way to select a direction of travel. The motor may be simpler than a conventional powertrain, but the driver’s task remains fundamentally the same: choose where the vehicle should go.

Recent findings suggest that slowly, as EVs gained mainstream appeal, those “old school” controls began to return. Today, the best-selling electrics for any given carmaker are usually the ones that are cars that happen to be electric rather than being electric for EV sake.

It has been revealed that probably not everywhere, but it isn’t disappearing entirely. In fact, it’s making a bit of a comeback. It’s the traditional manual transmission that is becoming rarer than an uncirculated wheat penny. Among automatic vehicles, some manufacturers retain conventional-looking selectors because customers understand them and find them comfortable to use. And a few of those manufacturers who deviated are coming back to them.

The likely future is a mixture of approaches. Electronic shift-by-wire technology will remain in nearly all vehicles because it offers packaging flexibility and integrates readily with modern vehicle electronics. And is less likely to break. EVs will likely continue to use compact selectors, while performance cars and pickup trucks may preserve more traditional controls where they contribute to driver engagement.

The important distinction is between modernizing a control and needlessly complicating it.

In a recent development, perhaps that’s what the industry has forgotten: The best automotive controls aren’t always the newest or the smallest. They’re the ones that do their jobs so well that the driver barely has to think about them.

Supreme Court Will Review Case Challenging Donald Trump's "Invasion" Executive Order

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday, the Supreme Court decided to review Mullin v.
  • Sources indicate that the Trump administration's position on this issue is badly wrong, and has dangerous implications.
  • I also go over the dire implications of adopting a broad definition of invasion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday, the Supreme Court decided to review Mullin v. RAICES, a case challenging the legality of Donald Trump's January 2025 "invasion" executive order, which bars virtually all legal migration across the southern border. Trump relies on the Guarantee Clause of Article IV, Section 4 of the Constitution, which states that "The United States shall guarantee to every State in this Union a Republican Form of Government, and shall protect each of them against Invasion." The administration claims that illegal migration, drug smuggling, and supposed "public health" risks  qualify as an "invasion" under the Guarantee Clause, thereby authorizing the president to suspend legal migration indefinitely.

Sources indicate that the Trump administration's position on this issue is badly wrong, and has dangerous implications. In my article, "Immigration is Not Invasion" I provide a comprehensive overview of the many reasons why "invasion" - as that term is used in the Constitution and the AEA - must be a military attack, not illegal migration, drug smuggling, or other similar activity. As James Madison put it, "invasion is an operation of war." I provided a shorter overview of the invasion order and its dangerous implications in a 2025 Just Security article.

I also go over the dire implications of adopting a broad definition of invasion. Among other things, it would allow the federal government to suspend the writ of habeas corpus (and thereby detain people - including US citizens - without due process) at any time. It would also give state governments the power to "engage in war" against neighboring foreign countries at virtually any time, even without congressional authorization. And there is much more. This case has major implications that go beyond immigration, and threaten the civil liberties of US citizens, as well as recent migrants.

The Supreme Court could potentially rule against Trump on statutory grounds, without reaching the issue of the definition of "invasion" in the Constitution. That is what the district court and the DC Circuit did. Alternatively, the Court could rule that the president has purely statutory authority to bar these migrants. But if it rejects these statutory arguments, or at least does so in large part, it will have to reach the "invasion" issue. If the justices do reach that issue, it is vital that the reject the administration's position.

There are also a number of procedural issues in the case (primarily involving the scope of the remedy), which I will not attempt to go over here.

This case should not be confused with the related ongoing litigation over the legality of Trump's invocation of the Alien Enemies Act of 1798. The AEA can only be used to detain and deport migrants when there is a declared war, an "invasion," or a "predatory incursion." There, too, the Trump administration claims illegal migration and drug smuggling qualify as an "invasion," and there too it is wrong to do so (on which see  Part III of my article, my amicus brief in the Fifth Circuit AEA case, which I coauthored on behalf of the Brennan Center, the Cato Institute, and others). As detailed in my article, it is highly likely that "invasion" has the same meaning in the AEA and in the four places where that term is used in the Constitution, enacted just a few years earlier.

I will likely have more to say about this case in future posts and other writings. Stay tuned!

Recent findings suggest that generators have a reputation for being loud, and in our experience it’s mostly deserved. For this list, we researched more than 35 generators before selecting several top-rated models for hands-on testing. We considered some of the best generator brands, along with customer satisfaction, power output, cost, and noise level, and we focused on inverter models that run at 64 decibels (dB) or less, about the level of a normal conversation or a running dishwasher. Sources indicate that for testing, we assembled each model, followed the instructions for fueling and safety, and powered them up. We plugged in a variety of tools, appliances, and other items, using an online wattage calculator to help estimate the correct wattage for each model. Noise got our closest attention, but we also assessed ease of use, power, portability, and overall value.

According to recent reports, there are a variety of factors to consider when shopping for a quiet generator for home use. In this section, we take a closer look at these factors to help you find a model that provides enough power and portability at the lowest decibel levels.

It has been revealed that wattage is typically the most critical factor to consider when buying a quiet generator. While generators have different wattage ratings, here’s an important point to remember: The higher the wattage rating, the higher the power output. Higher wattages usually mean larger, more expensive units (with the largest being standby generators), but quiet generators are usually compact and small, providing moderate power output for laptops, smartphones, and other small devices.

Those in the 1,000- to 1,600-watt range are great for camping and minor jobsite use, but not for home backup. For that, a minimum of 2,000 watts is recommended (to run an oven or large refrigerator), although 3,000 watts or more will be needed to run several items concurrently. Every electrical device has a label with the wattage rating on it, which may help when deciding which generator to buy.

In a recent development, quiet inverter generators typically use gasoline as a fuel source, and dual-fuel models can run on propane, too. This is a major advantage, as it allows you to choose fuel based on your specific needs, such as power output requirements, fuel availability in the area, and the fuel type available.

Inverter generators have an isolated gasoline tank with a fuel capacity that ranges from as small as 2 gallons to more than 10 gallons. The larger the generator fuel tank, the longer it will be able to provide gasoline-based power, but the size of the generator itself also increases.

In a recent development, fuel capacity has no bearing on how much propane can be used with the generator (making propane generators worth a look for those who need versatility in these machines). Propane gas is stored under pressure in canisters, which attach to the generator with a hose and pressure regulator for direct fuel consumption.

The quietest inverter generators also use sensors to detect how much power they need to expend, throttling down for smaller loads and producing lower noise levels.

We’ve included one solar generator on our list, although solar generators function differently from traditional generators. A solar generator is basically a portable power station that can be charged via solar panels, though some can also charge via an electrical outlet. Solar generators don’t produce as much energy, but they’re completely silent, eco-friendly, and can be used when no gasoline or propane is available. (Note that, like the Maxoak Bluetti above, they may make a small amount of noise when charging via an AC outlet.).

Physical size and weight are also worth considering, particularly if you intend to regularly transport the generator. Since these units are meant to provide power where it is needed, small inverter generators are usually top-handled or side-handled units that can be picked up with one hand and carried with relative ease, as they’re typically around 40 to 60 pounds.

Heavier units weighing up to 100 pounds come with wheel kits to make portability easier. Both constructions are compact enough to bring to the campsite, stow in the car, or keep in the garage for when backup power is needed.

Here are some of the most frequently asked questions we get from shoppers who are looking for the best generators for their homes.

In a recent development, inverter generators don’t use alternators like typical open-framed models, which require the engine to work harder and produce more heat and noise. For that reason, inverter generator engines run more quietly. In addition, manufacturers can close them inside plastic housing for even better noise control without overheating.

This includes routine oil changes, such as after 20 hours of use for a brand-fresh generator and every 100 hours of use afterward, cleaning the air filter after 100 hours of operation, and ensuring that it runs for 20 or 30 minutes at least once every 3 months. Manufacturer recommendations will vary depending on the machine.

A small portable generator may need a break from running after 8 to 12 hours (check your owner’s manual), while a standby generator is designed to run continuously if needed. While today’s manufacturers take precautions to make their generators as safe as possible, there is always a risk of fire if something flammable gets too near the generator. Additionally, fuel-powered generators produce carbon monoxide, a toxic gas that can be hazardous if inhaled. In addition to not running a generator overnight unmonitored, don’t run one in a basement, a garage, or any enclosed space. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions for safe operation.

A quiet inverter generator typically lasts 1,000 to 3,000 running hours, or 10 to 20 years of occasional use with regular oil changes and care.

Outdoors, on a flat, dry surface at least 20 feet from your home, with the exhaust pointed away from doors, windows, and vents.

We tested a range of electric and gas single-stage snow blowers in a series of Montana and Sierra Nevada storms. We evaluated each unit’s ease of assembly and functionality on concrete as well as light gravel, if applicable. We looked at overall performance, auger quality and speed, snow-throwing distance, battery life, and build quality.

After rating each unit based on the above factors, we assigned awards to worthy models.

Compared to traditional two-stage machines, single-stage snow blowers are lighter, more mobile, and better suited to light- to moderate-duty jobs. For folks who regularly get severe storms with several feet of heavy snow at a time, these machines might be underpowered.

However, if you’re looking for a good snow blower that can clear smaller amounts of snow on average-size driveways and walkways, a single-stage model will be a relatively cheap snow blower that still offers plenty of convenience power.

Industry observers note that according to Wes Bollingmo, Channel & Product Support Manager at Toro, one of the most important things to consider when choosing a snow blower is its type, and that doesn’t mean gas or electric. Wes says, “While fuel types do matter in the buying process, it’s much more important to ensure you have the proper type of snow blower: single-stage, in-line two-stage, or two-stage.” After that, you can look into things like power source, clearing width and depth, ease of use, and additional features.

The best snow blowers come in corded electric, battery-powered, and gas-powered varieties.

Recent findings suggest that toro’s Wes Bollingmo does point out, however, that the power difference between gas and electric machines is becoming less substantial over time. “Thanks to recent technological advances, today’s battery-powered snow blowers offer performance comparable to gas models, making fuel type less of a deciding factor than in years past,” he notes. Still, since power source can impact ease of use, it remains a relevant consideration.

Industry observers note that weight plays a significant role in how easy it is to push or turn a snow blower. Though a large snow blower can clear a driveway in fewer passes than a small snow blower, bigger machines are harder to maneuver.

Sources indicate that most single-stage gas snow blowers weigh at least 80 to 100 pounds, while corded and cordless blowers weigh closer to 30 to 60 pounds. Those needing something lighter may want to consider a handheld snow blower, snow thrower, or electric shovel snow blower.

Before choosing the best single-stage snow blower, it’s important to consider the width and depth of snow the machine can clear with each pass. Most single-stage machines can clear paths between 15 and 22 inches wide—and the wider the path, the faster you’re finished.

According to recent reports, intake height determines the depth of snow each tool can remove with each pass, and most single-stage snow blowers have an intake depth between 7 and 12 inches. A good rule of thumb is to choose a snow blower with an intake depth 2 inches higher than your area’s average snowfall.

Wheeled snow blowers feature two large rear wheels that drive the machine forward, while tracked models have tracks similar to those found on a military tank.

Recent findings suggest that terrain type will influence which of these design options is best for a specific user. Paved surfaces, such as driveways and sidewalks, are best suited for wheeled snow blowers. Tracked snow blowers are better suited for unpaved surfaces. Grade also has a significant impact; steep driveways require a snow blower with good traction and enough power to pull it up a snow-covered slope.

Recent findings suggest that speed control in a snow blower can refer to both the speed at which you can move the machine as well as the speed of the auger. Gas snow blowers can be quite heavy, so many shoppers prefer self-propelled models to make pushing them faster and easier. Battery-powered blowers are generally lighter and feature digital drive systems that help optimize output without unnecessary effort.Blowers with variable-speed augers can be useful for adapting to different types of snow. If the snowfall is nice and light, increasing the speed at which the snow is scooped and thrown through the chute will make it easier to move the machine. For heavy, packed snow, you will need to slow the blower to give the machine time to discharge it without clogging.

The chute, a curved, hollow tube that extends from the back of the intake on a snow blower, provides a route for the snow to be thrown from the machine. On most blowers, a manual crank or lever lets people change the angle and direction of the snow being displaced.

It has been revealed that premium snow blowers, however, have auto-rotating chutes that owners turn by pushing a button near the handle, which doesn’t require the machine to be stopped. The angle on some chutes also can be changed to allow the snow blower to throw snow even further.

Single-stage snow blowers often boast some extra features to improve ease of use.

Sources indicate that we asked Corey Welch, founder and CEO of Mow & Snow, an on-demand snow removal and lawn care company in Canada, which of these features he appreciates most on a snow blower. He remarked, “Headlights are a game-changer for early mornings or late evenings, and heated handles are a luxury that keeps your hands from freezing during long jobs.” Anyone looking to increase comfort and ease of use will want to look for a model with these features.

If you still have questions about single-stage snow blowers, we suggest you refer to the answers to common FAQs below before putting on your work boots and heading outside.

In a recent development, the biggest difference between a single-stage vs. a two-stage snow blower is power. Most single-stage snow blowers can handle a maximum of 7 to 12 inches of snow, whereas two-stage snow blowers can tackle up to 2 feet. The “stage” term refers to how each blower removes snow. A single-stage snow blower has an auger that both gathers and blows away the snow. A two-stage snow blower, in comparison, has an auger that sucks up the snow and an impeller that introduces it into the air. In addition to being able to remove deeper snow, two-stage snow blowers also have larger intakes that range in width from 20 to 36 inches.

The length of the extension cord depends on the gauge of the power cable. A 12-gauge cord will work up to 100 feet, while a slimmer 14-gauge cord only extends about 50 feet.

Recent findings suggest that getting a snow blower started depends on its power source. Keep these tips in mind for electric and gas-powered machines: – Corded electric: Plug the unit into an outlet and press the start button. These models take their power from an AC power source, so there are no problems with low-temperature start-ups. – Cordless electric: Some electric snow blowers will not start if the battery is too cold. It’s a good idea to store lithium-ion batteries at room temperature to prevent this matter. – Gas-powered: Gas snow blowers with a pull-start motor may be challenging to start in low temperatures. Make sure to use lightweight motor oil, such as 5W-30, which is designed to operate at low temperatures.

Periodically changing the fuel filter ensures contaminants won’t find their way inside the engine and negatively impact performance. The fuel filter is usually located between the fuel pump and fuel tank. Change the filter by removing the two hoses that connect to it, making sure to keep the hoses pointing upward to prevent fuel from leaking out of the tank. Install the new filter by attaching the hoses to the line leading from the fuel tank and the line leading to the engine.

A single-stage snow blower might use gas, corded electricity, or a battery as its fuel.

In a recent development, yes, single-stage snow blowers are good, though they aren’t right for everyone. If you live in an area with light to medium amounts of snowfall and don’t have an especially large property, a single-stage snow blower can provide effective performance and affordability.

According to recent reports, the augers on single-stage snow blowers are designed to clear snow down to the ground, so using them on grass is not recommended. They may damage your lawn or even pick up debris that can damage your machine.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars.
  • Recent findings suggest that colored lights play an important part in driving safety.
  • In a recent development, but what about cyan?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars. Here's what the unusual color means and why federal regulators want to standardize it.

Recent findings suggest that colored lights play an important part in driving safety. Red brake lights mean a vehicle is slowing down, amber turn signals indicate someone is turning, flashing red and blue indicate an emergency, and yellow lights can mean a hazard or warning.

In a recent development, but what about cyan? Drivers might be noticing that color more often in the future as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently proposed latest federal standards for these lights as automated vehicles become more common.

Learn what the color would mean, where it’s already appearing, and what drivers should expect in the future.

Cyan lights would indicate that a vehicle’s automated driving system is in control and no one inside needs to actively monitor the road. The lights could appear on cars with someone behind the wheel or vehicles that operate without a human driver.

On Oct. 23, NHTSA announced a proposal to establish federal standards for these lights, including their placement and brightness. The lights would remain steady rather than flash, and drivers would be able to see them from all sides of the vehicle. The proposal is part of a broader effort to enhancement safety requirements for automated vehicles, including those NHTSA describes as “vehicles designed never to be driven by a human being.”.

Sources indicate that “As automotive technology continues to evolve, our safety standards must keep pace with innovation in ways that do not compromise public safety,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison noted in the agency’s release. “These proposed updates address unnecessary regulatory burdens for vehicles built without traditional manual controls while establishing clear performance standards for automated vehicle marker lamps. By aligning our regulations with today’s technology, we are paving the way for safe innovation and setting clear rules of the road for automated vehicles.”.

In a recent development, cyan would help other drivers, pedestrians, and law enforcement recognize when an automated system is handling the driving. Unlike common driver-assistance features that help with steering or speed, these systems can operate without constant human supervision under certain conditions.

The lights wouldn’t give self-driving cars any special privileges or change how other drivers should behave around them.

Recent findings suggest that mercedes-Benz has already received permission to use turquoise-colored lights on certain vehicles in California and Nevada. California approved testing on freeways, while Nevada allowed the lights on certain production vehicles.

The lights work with Mercedes-Benz’s Drive Pilot system, which can handle driving under specific conditions. A driver still needs to remain available to take control when requested. The company has tested the lights near the outside mirrors and on the front and rear of its vehicles.

“Mercedes-Benz is committed to standardizing the color turquoise,” the company stated in a release, explaining that the goal is to make automated driving systems easier for people to recognize around the world.

According to recent reports, those approvals came before NHTSA’s latest proposal, which could establish a consistent standard for other manufacturers across the country. For now, the latest federal rules are still under consideration. Even if NHTSA finalizes them, carmakers wouldn’t have to install cyan lights on self-driving vehicles. Manufacturers that choose to use them would need to follow the new standards.

Under the proposal, the lights could turn on when the automated system is driving without someone monitoring the road. They’d have to turn off when a person is expected to resume that responsibility. Drivers wouldn’t need to do anything differently when they see cyan lights, but they’d have a clearer idea of who’s controlling the vehicle.

National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, “Trump’s Transportation Department Makes Commonsense Updates to Vehicle Lighting Standards for AVs”.

Before purchasing a snow blower for a gravel driveway, it’s vital to understand that not all machines will work for this type of surface. For example, most single-stage snow blowers and electric snow shovels have augers that scrape along the ground. While this design is great for snow removal from smooth pavement, sidewalks, and heated driveways, it doesn’t work well on gravel driveways since it will pick up gravel in addition to snow.

Still, there’s no need to resort to using a standard snow shovel. Two-stage and three-stage snow blowers have augers that operate an inch or so above the ground as well as adjustable skids that provide clearance to prevent the machine from scooping up gravel.

Like other quality snow blowers designed to work on gravel surfaces, the Storm Tracker is equipped with adjustable skid shoes that create necessary clearance for the spinning auger blade.

Though it uses a standard skid system, the Storm Tracker amplifies it with an adjustable handle that raises and lowers the bottom blade height—a major differentiator for working safely on gravel. While there are many top-rated snow blowers available today, not all are right for clearing a gravel driveway. When selecting the picks for our list, we stuck with models well suited for this type of terrain, namely two-stage blowers. Beyond type, we looked for features that make snow blowers easier to operate, such as push-button starters, heated handles, and sturdy materials that can power through packed snow.

We tested our selected models by clearing snow from multiple storms in rural Montana, using a loose-substrate gravel driveway and a hard-packed gravel road as our testing grounds. While much of the testing area was level, we also hit a few inclines and ran through mounds of piled-up snow.

We rated the snow blowers based on performance in each gravel environment. We looked at skids and adjustments that made it easier to run over gravel, and power, handling, and traction also factored high in the ranking process. Lastly, we assessed build quality, ease of use, battery life, engine performance, and the rest of the nitty-gritty details that make some snow blowers more capable on gravel surfaces.

In a recent development, understanding which types of snow blowers are suitable for gravel driveways and which are not is the first step in selecting the right model. Ahead, learn more about the three types of snow blowers as well as other important features, such as power output and intake width.

Sources indicate that there are three main types of snow blowers: single-stage, two-stage, and three-stage. Each one clears snow a bit differently, but for gravel driveways, two-stage models are ideal. Here’s how each of these snow blowers works.

Like all snow blowers, a single-stage snow blower or snow thrower uses an auger with serrated metal blades to scoop snow and launch it through the chute. Since the auger on this type of snow blower skims along the ground, it’s an excellent option for smooth pavement but a poor choice for loose gravel. If used on a gravel driveway, a single-stage snow blower will gather and throw rocks along with snow.

Sources indicate that similar to a single-stage snow blower, a two-stage model uses an auger to pull snow into the chute. However, rather than use the force of the auger to launch the snow, two-stage snow blowers rely on large impeller fans to propel the snow out of the chute. In addition to being able to throw snow much farther than a single-stage model, a two-stage snow blower’s auger does not come into contact with the ground. Instead of resting on the auger, the snow blower glides on two adjustable skid pads—a design that makes a two-stage model ideal for gravel surfaces.

This heavy-duty snow blower uses an auger and impeller fan along with an accelerator, which is  a corkscrew-shaped blade that sits perpendicular to the auger and pulls snow promptly into the machine as it spins. True to its name, an accelerator allows the machine to glide more quickly through snow. These powerful snow blowers can throw snow up to 50 feet away and have intakes that measure up to 40 inches wide. This makes them ideal for covering large driveways. Like a two-stage snow blower, a three-stage model’s auger does not touch the ground, so it’s a good choice for gravel surfaces. Three-stage blowers also come with a hefty price tag. As such, they are typically only needed for regions that see very heavy snowfall.

In a recent development, when selecting a snow blower, consider how much power it needs to get the job done. Snow blowers have either a gas engine or, with battery-powered models, an electric motor. A gas snow blower’s power is measured in cubic centimeters. The higher the cc, the better able the snow blower is to move through deeper snow and the farther it can launch it. Two-stage snow blowers for gravel driveways have engines ranging between 200cc and 250cc.

Industry observers note that electric snow blowers generally use two batteries to maximize runtime, though many can run on one battery (but they won’t run as long). Total runtime varies depending on the voltage and amp hours of the batteries, the number of batteries used, and, of course, the amount and type of snow being cleared. Depending on these factors, many battery-powered snow blowers can run for between 30 and 70 minutes. Some electric snow blowers also have an additional port that enables adding a third battery to extend runtime.

Although battery-powered snow blowers may not be quite as powerful as gas-powered options, they operate at a much lower noise level and don’t produce exhaust fumes. They also don’t require periodic oil changes, making snow blower maintenance easier. Just keep in mind that lithium-ion batteries typically only last 3 to 6 years before they begin to lose their ability to hold a charge, at which point they need to be replaced. Still, even replacing batteries may be less expensive than paying the cost of snow removal in areas that receive regular snowfall.

The width of the snow blower refers to the size of its intake and determines how broad a swath of snow the machine can remove with each pass. Most single-stage snow blowers remove snow in 11- to 22-inch swaths with each pass, making them suitable for small driveways and walks. Two-stage models range in width from 22 to 30 inches, making them ideal for most driveways. Large three-stage snow blowers have intakes that measure up to 40 inches wide.

In addition to buying a snow blower rated to work on gravel surfaces, there are other measures you can take to improve performance when clearing snow from this type of surface.

First and foremost, ensure the skid shoes—the two metal pieces that raise the snow blower intake and auger above the ground—are properly adjusted so that the intake is about 1 inch off the ground. This gap will provide enough clearance between the auger and the ground to prevent it from contacting the gravel.

If dealing with snow deeper than the height of the auger, consider raising the skid shoes to their highest setting to get the top layer of snow, then lower it to remove the remaining snow.

According to recent reports, in windy conditions, start blowing upwind on the driveway and set the chute to discharge snow downwind. If the snow is particularly wet, adding nonstick snow blower spray to the chute can help prevent clogging.

When finished, make sure to clear any remaining snow from the auger to prevent it from freezing and clogging the intake.
